keyQuestionRatings.name: Effective
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Effective – this means we looked for evidence that people’s care, treatment and support achieved good outcomes and promoted a good quality of life, based on best available evidence. At our last assessment we rated this key question requires improvement. At this assessment the rating has changed to good. This meant people’s outcomes were consistently good, and people’s feedback confirmed this.

People were supported to make decisions and be in control of their lives. People attended healthcare appointments and were supported to receive treatment.

topicareas.name: Assessing needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider made sure people’s care and treatment was effective by assessing and reviewing their health, care, wellbeing and communication needs with them. There were effective processes in place to assess people’s needs to make sure the service could meet people’s needs. Before people started using the service, they had a face to face meeting with the registered manager, with support and in a place they were comfortable.

The assessment process included all areas of the person’s support including the hours of 1:1 support. The accommodation on offer is shared, part of the assessment is to look at if the person would be compatible to live with the other person. There was a transition process for people when they moved into the accommodation. This included day visits and overnight stays, people would then be offered the choice of keyworker based on their needs and interests. The process of moving into the accommodation is taken at the pace of the person.

When a person’s needs could not be met by the service, the provider’s other services would be considered and offered as an alternative for consideration.

People’s support plans and goals were kept under review, keyworkers reviewed plans at least monthly or when people’s needs changed. Staff worked with people’s GPs to review their medicines regularly.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Consent to care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider told people about their rights around consent and respected these when delivering person-centred care and treatment. Staff understood their responsibilities to support people, when needed to make decisions. People receiving support from the service had been assessed as being able to make day to day decisions. People told us they made decisions about all areas of their lives. They explained to us how they planned their meals with staff and shopped for them.

People were assessed as being safe to go out unaccompanied. However, some people preferred to go out with staff for reassurance. When people made unwise decisions, staff supported them by making sure they were as safe as possible. Staff told us “If they want to do it, we will find the safest way to do it without restrictions.”

Staff had completed best interest decisions when complex decisions were needed such as moving or having surgery. When people did not have family to support and advise them, professionals who knew people well, were involved to make sure the decision was in their best interest. Staff used videos, easy reads and information from reliable sources such as the NHS website.

Staff understood how people’s moods and emotions could affect their capacity to make decisions. Staff completed capacity assessments following conversations with people to record their advanced decisions. For example, a person knew they would make certain decisions when they were feeling unwell, such as not being taken to hospital. The person recognised this was not a decision they would make if they were well. Staff had informed them when they lacked capacity, and they would act to keep them safe.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Delivering evidence-based care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider planned and delivered people’s care and treatment with them, including what was important and mattered to them. They did this in line with legislation and current evidence-based good practice and standards. Each person had a support plan which included nationally recognised tools such as Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST) to identify risks and guidance to reduce the risk. Staff had followed the guidance in the tools including referrals to healthcare professionals.

People’s support plans included person centred goals they wished to achieve and how they this would be supported. People were supported to manage their health conditions such as diabetes following national evidence based guidance. Staff told us how they supported people to follow guidance and adapted their routines to help with this.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: How staff, teams and services work together

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider worked well across teams and services to support people. The service worked with other professionals across all aspects of people’s support. Staff made sure health professionals were kept informed of what other professionals had prescribed, or action taken.

Staff had negotiated systems with professionals like the district nurse, so people were supported. For example, one person did not like having their injection from staff. A system was in place for the district nurse to give the injection, and a non-invasive procedure was agreed to enable staff to monitor the person’s health. Other people had complex health needs and staff co-ordinated their health support including having professionals come to their home as they were more comfortable with this.

People had hospital passports in place. These were taken to any appointments or when people went into hospital, to make sure people received their support according to their preferences.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Monitoring and improving outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider routinely monitored people’s care and treatment to continuously improve it. They ensured that outcomes were positive and consistent, and that they met both clinical expectations and the expectations of people themselves. Staff knew people well and understood how to support them in situations which may cause them anxiety. Staff had liaised with the GP to support a person with regular blood tests. The person chose which staff member they wanted to support them along with a family member and numbing cream was applied to the area. This process had transformed the person’s experience. Another person had a good understanding of their various medical conditions but could become very anxious when going to appointments. A system had been agreed whereby they booked all the transport etc. and then checked with staff it was correct. They had also requested staff to go with them to give them confidence as they know staff will advocate for them if needed. They also discussed the appointments afterwards to make sure the person understood what had happened and they were happy with the outcome.

Staff had helped people build people’s confidence to go for health checks. People were now confident to go to the dentist with staff support as they were now less anxious. People went to a local optician who used pictures for people who could not recognise letters when testing their vision.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Supporting people to live healthier lives

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider supported people to manage their health and wellbeing to maximise their independence, choice and control. Staff supported people to live healthier lives and where possible, reduce their future needs for care and support. People explained to us the healthy choices they made around meals. One person explained how they had low sugar options as they were diabetic and ate brown bread, “Because it is healthier.” They told us how staff had supported them to understand their blood sugar levels. The person and staff used the same process to lower the person’s blood sugar such as drinking water and going for a walk. They told us how they had requested money rather than chocolate for Easter, this was better for them, and they were saving up for something.

People had access to an optician and dentist. People were registered with dentists which specialise in supporting people living with learning disability. People’s confidence to go to the dentist had been built up over a period time. The dentists had worked with staff and people to decide the least restrictive options reducing the need for sedation to complete any work.

Some people had a gym membership, they had completed training around healthy diets, some people had attended weight loss classes.

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Well-led – this means we looked for evidence that service leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation; and promoted an open, fair culture. At our last assessment we rated this key question requires improvement. At this assessment the rating has changed to good. This meant the service was consistently managed and well-led. Leaders and the culture they created promoted high-quality, person-centred care.

The registered manager had oversight of the service and monitored the quality. Staff were confident to speak up and concerns would be dealt with.

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider had inclusive leaders at all levels who understood the context in which they delivered care, treatment and support and embodied the culture and values of their workforce and organisation. Leaders had the skills, knowledge, experience and credibility to lead effectively. They did so with integrity, openness and honesty. Staff told us they felt supported by the management team. There were regular staff meetings, where any concerns were discussed and senior management attended if requested.

Staff told us their continued development was supported, and they knew they had a career path. The provider identified the skills staff needed to support people and made sure they were offered this training.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider fostered a positive culture where people felt they could speak up and their voice would be heard. The provider has ‘Speak Up Guardians’ in place, to support staff to raise concerns outside of the service.

Staff told us they felt listened to by the management team and they operated an ‘open door’ policy. Staff were confident any concerns they had would be dealt with appropriately. Staff knew how to raise concerns with outside agencies if needed. Staff told us when they had raised concerns, “They were dealt with professionally.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider had clear responsibilities, roles, systems of accountability and good governance. There were effective processes in place to monitor the quality of the service. The registered manager completed audits on all areas of the service. Monthly audits were completed on support plans, medicines, compliance and people’s finance. When shortfalls were found an action plan was developed, including who was responsible and the date the action needed to be completed by. Staff updated the action plan when they completed an action.

Staff understood their responsibilities and roles. There was a clear staff structure and staff we spoke with knew who they were accountable to and their role in supporting people.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider focused on continuous learning, innovation and improvement across the organisation and local system. They encouraged creative ways of delivering equality of experience, outcome and quality of life for people. The provider supported a proactive system to learn from incidents across all their services and were open to staff raising concerns.

The registered manager kept up to date with any changes in the social care environment and used this information to encourage change and improvement for people being supported by the service.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider understood their duty to collaborate and work in partnership, so services worked seamlessly for people. They shared information and learning with partners and collaborated for improvement. The provider was a member of local forums and shaping the future groups. The managers of all their services had access to Skills for Care and the latest information and guidance.

Staff had worked with community services such as dentists, opticians and GPs to make them accessible for people living with a learning disability.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider had a shared vision, strategy and culture. This was based on transparency, equity, equality and human rights, diversity and inclusion, engagement, and understanding challenges and the needs of people and their communities. Staff understood the aims of the service, “Support independence, support people to make decisions and live a fulfilling life” and “Live their best possible lives.” Staff explained how they worked to meet the aims including supporting people to make decisions and to do as much as possible such go on holidays.

The providers values underpin all aspects of the service, it was discussed at staff supervisions and how staff demonstrated the values in their work.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider valued diversity in their workforce. They worked towards an inclusive and fair culture by improving equality and equity for people who worked for them. There were policies in place to promote equality, diversity and inclusion. Staff thought they were treated equally, and their cultural heritage was embraced. Staff told us, “Staff from different backgrounds bring different experiences”. There was a Nigerian evening recently for all staff in Kent. Staff told us there were no barriers because of age, “I feel my experience is valued and there are opportunities for development if I want them.”

asgRatings.title: Ongoing Assessment for K D Care Limited
asgRatings.name: Homecare
asgRatings.commentary:
We completed an inspection between 15 September and 30 September 2025. K D Care Limited is a domiciliary care service providing the regulated activity of personal care to people in their own homes. We inspected the service due to length of time since the last inspection. We assessed the service against ‘Right support, right care, right culture’ guidance to make judgements about whether the provider guaranteed people with a learning disability and autistic people respect, equality, dignity, choices, independence and good access to local communities that most people take for granted. The service was not meeting the guidance of RSRCRC: this had a detrimental impact on people’s lives. There was a closed culture at the service. A "closed culture" is a poor culture that can lead to harm, including human rights breaches and abuse. We found a poor culture across the entire service, which had not been recognised or addressed by the provider.

The provider failed to ensure people’s health risks were well managed, and people were not supported by suitably qualified and competent staff. Medicines had not been managed safely. People were not treated with dignity, kindness and respect. There was no oversight of the service to identify and make improvements. There were no audits or checks in place to identify the significant concerns we found during the inspection. The provider was also the registered manager of the service.

We found significant shortfalls across the service and identified breaches of 7 regulations in relation to providing people with person centred care, safeguarding, safe care and treatment, need for consent, staffing, dignity and respect and good governance.

This service is being placed in special measures. The purpose of special measures is to ensure that services providing inadequate care make significant improvements. Special measures provide a framework within which we user our enforcement powers in response to inadequate care and provide a timeframe within which providers must improve the quality of the care they provide. In instances where CQC have decided to take civil or criminal enforcement action against a provider, we will publish this information on our website after any representations and/or appeals have been concluded.
asgRatings.narrative: The service is performing badly and we've taken action against the person or organisation that runs it.
asgRatings.overallPeopleExperience:
People’s relatives told us they were not always happy with the care provided by K D Care Limited. For example, one relative told us. ‘I was pleased CQC were investigating in the background, I didn’t feel it was safe at all.’

Our assessment found elements of care did not meet the expected standards. For example, people’s health and wellbeing risks were not being well managed. This included people’s health conditions not being managed well. People were not supported to have full control and choices in relation to the care and support they received.

keyQuestionRatings.name: Caring
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Caring – this means we looked for evidence that the provider involved people and treated them with compassion, kindness, dignity and respect. At our last assessment we rated this key question good. At this assessment the rating has changed to requires improvement. However, the quality statements we assessed: Independence, choice and control were scored as inadequate. This meant people did not always feel well-supported, cared for or treated with dignity and respect.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to person centred care.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always caring

topicareas.name: Independence, choice and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not promote people’s independence, so people did not know their rights and have choice and control over their own care, treatment and wellbeing. Care and support plans contained very little detail on how staff could support people to be as independent as possible. For example, care plans did not contain goals that were specific to them or how staff could support them to set short term or long term goals.

People were not always supported or encouraged to access activities and go out to promote and support their independence, health and wellbeing. For example, 1 person’s care plan detailed, ‘It is extremely important’ that the person was supported to go out for their wellbeing.’ The daily notes described on a number of occasions where person ‘laid in bed all day’. There was no record of how staff encouraged and supported people with the choices they had made.

keyQuestionRatings.name: Effective
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Effective – this means we looked for evidence that people’s care, treatment and support achieved good outcomes and promoted a good quality of life, based on best available evidence. At our last assessment we rated this key question good. At this assessment the rating has changed to requires improvement. However, the quality statements we assessed: Assessing needs and Consent to care and treatment were scored as inadequate. This meant the effectiveness of people’s care, treatment and support did not always achieve good outcomes or was inconsistent.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to consent and person-centred care.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always effective

topicareas.name: Assessing needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not make sure people’s care and treatment was effective because they did not check and discuss people’s health, care, wellbeing and communication needs with them. The provider failed to ensure peoples needs were fully assessed. For example, 1 person’s care plan detailed they now required a walking aid. The provider had not implemented an assessment around the persons mobility or assessed if they were at risk of falling. The provider told us they had reviewed the care plans prior to our inspection but they had not identified the areas that were missing regarding peoples needs.

People’s communication needs were not fully assessed, which meant the effectiveness of their care could not be maximised. The provider had failed to assess and review people’s communication needs and take action if it was needed.

The provider had not ensured people, and their relatives were involved with care planning. One person’s relative told us, ‘No one had ever got me involved, I don’t think [persons] needs were ever reviewed.’

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Consent to care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not tell people about their rights around consent or respect these when delivering care and treatment. The provider failed to ensure that people’s capacity was assessed in line with the Mental Capacity Act 2005. People’s care plans did not include information regarding their capacity and how staff can support them when making decisions about their care.

One person had monitors in place to support them with their seizures to alert staff. However, the provider had not ensured that capacity assessments had been carried out to ensure they were the least restrictive option in line with the Mental Capacity Act 2005.

The provider had not assured themselves that people’s legal representative or advocates could make decisions on their behalf in line with the Mental Capacity Act 2005. For example, the provider had not obtained evidence where people had a lasting power of attorney. An LPA, orLasting Power of Attorney isa legal document that allows people to appoint trusted individuals (attorneys) to make financial, property, health, and welfare decisions on their behalf if they lose mental capacity.The provider had not ensured that these arrangements were active and in line with the Mental capacity Act 2005.

topicareas.name: Equity in experiences and outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary: Staff and leaders did not listen to information about people who are most likely to experience inequality in experience or outcomes. This meant people’s care was not tailored in response to this. The provider could not demonstrate how they supported and promoted equality. The provider had not ensured that people were not exposed to unnecessary barriers when making decisions around their support. The provider had not assured themselves that legal representation, such as a power of attorney, for people was active and in place. For example, the provider told us that for one person, their relative made all decisions, however it was not documented what decisions the person could make for themselves.

topicareas.name: Person-centred Care

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not make sure people were at the centre of their care and treatment choices and they did not work in partnership with people, to decide how to respond to any relevant changes in people’s needs. People’s care plans did not reflect their physical, mental, emotional and social needs, including those related to protected characteristics under the Equality Act. For example, 1 person’s care plan detailed they had protective equipment to help prevent injuries. However, the care notes did not detail how staff had encouraged or supported the person to wear this or recorded discussions when the person has chosen not to wear the equipment.

One person’s care plan detailed they would like to do voluntary work. However, there was no plan in place on how staff were supporting them to achieve this.

Care plans did not fully consider people’s dignity and how staff could support them to maintain their dignity. For people who needed emergency interventions that could compromise their dignity, detailed guidance was not in place for staff to ensure they do everything possible to preserve people’s dignity.

keyQuestionRatings.name: Safe
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Safe – this means we looked for evidence that people were protected from abuse and avoidable harm. At our last assessment we rated this key question Good. At this assessment the rating has changed to inadequate. This meant people were not safe and were at risk of avoidable harm.

The service was in breach of legal regulations in relation to people’s safe care and treatment, safeguarding people from abuse and staffing.

topicareas.name: Infection prevention and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not assess or manage the risk of infection. They did not detect and control the risk of it spreading. The provider failed to ensure people’s care plans highlighted the risk or provided detailed mitigation around infection control. For example, care plans did not detail the risks around food hygiene safety and reheating food. Daily notes for one person recorded on multiple occasions, that ‘yesterdays takeaway was reheated for dinner’.

The provider also failed to evidence their assurances that staff were complying with IPC measures such as wearing personal protective equipment (PPE). The provider had not completed spots checks which included making sure staff were wearing the appropriate clothing and PPE.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Involving people to manage risks

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not work well with people to understand and manage risks. Staff did not provide care to meet people’s needs that was safe, supportive and enabled people to do the things that mattered to them. The provider failed to ensure support plans and guidance were in place to mitigate the risks relating to people’s health needs. The provider failed to manage peoples risks around epilepsy. For example, 1 person could experience multiple seizures and different types of seizures. The care plan did not provide staff with detailed information to support the person safely. The care plan did not provide clear guidance around what action staff needed to take in relation to the different types of seizures the person could experience. We identified instances where people’s seizures had not been managed in line with their care plan, placing them at risk of avoidable harm.

The provider failed to manage the risks around respiratory conditions. One person’s care plan detailed they were prescribed regular and ‘as required’ medicines for a respiratory condition. The provider had not implemented any guidance for staff on how to support the person with their health condition on a day to day basis or in an emergency situation.

The provider failed to manage people’s health risks in relation to mobility. For example, 1 person’s care plan detailed they required a walking aid. However, there was no other information to inform staff how to use the walking aid, when the walking aid should be used or environmental risks relating to the walking aid. People were at risk of their mobility needs not being met or not being well managed.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not have a proactive and positive culture of safety based on openness and honesty. They did not listen to concerns about safety and did not investigate or report safety events. Lessons were not learnt to continually identify and embed good practice. The provider failed to ensure action was taken when issues were identified. The provider told us they were aware of issues when they took over in March 2025, however they were not able to evidence what action they had taken to address these concerns.

Incidents and accidents were not fully reviewed and appropriate action taken to mitigate risks. For example, one incident had occurred in relation to medicines administration and the provider’s proposed action was for the staff member to be observed administering medicines. However, the provider had acquired an agency staff member to video call the staff member and observe them administering medicines. The provider had not assured themselves that the agency staff member was competent to carry out this task. The provider had failed to ensure actions taken following incidents mitigated the risks to people using the service.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Medicines optimisation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not make sure that medicines and treatments were safe and met people’s needs, capacities and preferences. People were not involved in planning. The provider failed to ensure that medicines were managed safely. We reviewed medication administration records (MAR) that were inaccurate and the provider told us they knew that the legal document was not being completed accurately. The provider told us that an agency staff member would video call staff whilst they administered medicines to act as a witness, the provider told us this was because staff were not competent to administer medicines. However, the provider did not have assurances that the agency staff member was competent and trained to oversee the administration of medication.

The provider failed to ensure people were involved with managing their medicines. The provider told us that one person had capacity, however they were not allowed to access their medicines, and they were locked away. The provider had not considered the person’s capacity or views in relation to their medication.

People who were prescribed ‘as required’ medicines did not have robust guidance in place. One person’s care plan did not provide clear instructions around when to administer their emergency medicines in relation to their epilepsy. The records showed that there were occasions where the person’s emergency medicine had not been administered in line with their protocol, this included the medicine being administered when it was not required and a larger does being administered than what was prescribed. We could not be assured that staff were administering the medicine appropriately or safely.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe and effective staffing

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not make sure there were enough qualified, skilled and experienced staff. They did not always make sure staff received effective support, supervision and development. They did not work together well to provide safe care that met people’s individual needs. The provider failed to ensure robust recruitment practices were in place to ensure staff were competent and safe to support people. The provider did not have recruitment files for the 3 staff that were employed, this meant the provider did not have information regarding references, interview questions, evidence of right to work in the UK, application forms or evidence of a Disclosure and barring service (DBS) check. A DBS check (Disclosure and Barring Service check) isa record that shows a person's criminal convictions and cautions, issued by the Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS) in England and Wales.It helps employers make safer hiring decisions. This meant the provider had no assurance that staff members did not have any recorded criminal convictions and were safe to work with vulnerable people.

There were not appropriate staffing levels to make sure people received consistently safe, good quality care that meets their needs. The provider told us that staff managed the rotas and breaks themselves and staff worked for 72 hours without a break or sleeping. People were supported by staff who were not well rested. This was unsafe for both people and staff and increased the likelihood of poor care.

The provider failed to ensure staff received appropriate training for their role. The provider was not able to evidence that staff had completed training in specialist areas which were required for their role. For example, the provider failed to ensure that staff were trained in administering emergency ‘as require’ medicines that were prescribed for people with epilepsy. The provider had not completed competency assessments for staff to ensure they were competent to carry out the care that was being delivered, even after incidents of medicine errors.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe environments

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not always detect and control potential risks in the care environment. The provider failed to ensure they carried out assessments of people’s homes to ensure any environmental risks were mitigated. For example, care and support plans did not detail risks around fire, such how to support people to safety in the event of a fire or where the escape routes are out of the property.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe systems, pathways and transitions

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not work well with people and health system partners to establish and maintain safe systems of care. They did not manage or monitor people’s safety. They did not make sure there was continuity of care, including when people moved between different services. For example, the provider had failed to review and assess peoples care and support when they took over the service. The provider had failed to ensure people’s view were taken into account and documented regarding their care and support.

The provider had not ensured people had hospital passports in place to ensure important information could be shared with other professionals, such as during hospital visits. A hospital passport isa personalised document created for people with learning disabilities, Autistic people, or other communication needs to help healthcare staff provide appropriate and effective care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safeguarding

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not work well with people and healthcare partners to understand what being safe meant to them and how to achieve that. They did not concentrate on improving people’s lives or protecting their right to live in safety, free from bullying, harassment, abuse, discrimination, avoidable harm and neglect. The provider failed to ensure safeguarding processes were in place to keep people from harm. The provider failed to demonstrate a strong understanding of safeguarding and they had not identified that people were at risk of neglect. For example, 1 person’s daily notes detailed, ‘they didn’t ask for dinner so I didn’t make them dinner.’ The provider also failed to take action when staff documented people refused their emergency prescribed medicines or personal care. When we highlighted our safeguarding concerns with the provider, they told us they felt there were no safeguarding concerns, which demonstrate their lack of understanding. During the inspection the provider informed us they could no longer provide safe care to people. The provider told us they had informed the local safeguarding team.

Relatives told us they did not always feel their loved one was safe. One relative told us, ‘I wasn’t happy [person] was safe.’

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Well-led – this means we looked for evidence that service leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation; and promoted an open, fair culture. At our last assessment we rated this key question Good. At this assessment the rating has changed to inadequate. This meant there were widespread and significant shortfalls in leadership. Leaders and the culture they created did not assure the delivery of high-quality care.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to good governance.

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not have inclusive leaders at all levels who understood the context in which they delivered care, treatment and support, or who embodied the culture and values of their workforce and organisation. Leaders did not have the skills, knowledge, experience and credibility to lead effectively, and they did not do so with integrity, openness and honesty. For example, the provider told us they had not completed any recruitment checks for the staff since they started at the service 6 months prior to the inspection. The provider had not assured themselves that the staff were capable and compassionate with the care they delivered.

The provider had notimplemented relevant or mandatory quality frameworks, recognised standards, best practices or equivalents to improve equity in experience and outcomes for people using services and tackle known inequalities. For example, the provider did not know what RSRCRC was and they had not followed or implemented the legislation around the Mental Capacity Act. The provider demonstrated a lack of knowledge in relation to these frameworks.

Leaders were not always alert to examples of poor culture or when it was identified, this was not addressed quickly. The provider failed to ensure they had process in place to identify training needs. The provider told us they were aware that there was missing information regarding training when they started, however they had not taken action to rectify this.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary: People did not always feel they could speak up and that their voice would be heard. Whilst some people told us they understood what freedom to speak up meant, it was not clear if people felt they would be listened to and action taken in response. The provider did not have the skills and competence to ensure that when concerns were raised, appropriate action was taken to address the concerns. For example, the provider was aware of concerns around staff conduct and poor practice but they had not taken action to fully understand or address the issues.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not have clear responsibilities, roles, systems of accountability and good governance. They did not act on the information about risk, performance and outcomes, or share this securely with others when appropriate. The provider was also the registered manager of the service. When we asked questions regarding the service and the people they supported they could not give us detailed answers in relation to their role. The registered manager did not understand their role and responsibilities as a provider and registered manager.

The provider failed to ensure effective governance systems were in place across all aspects of the service. The provider failed to ensure effective audits were carried out to identify the risks that we found during the assessment. We found widespread issues relating to incidents, safeguarding, medicines management, risk assessments, lack of person-centred care guidance, no recruitment checks, lack of training and support for staff and a disregard for legislation and frameworks such as MCA.

The provider had not understood their role and responsibilities as a provider and registered manager in relation to notifying the commission of changes. The provider told us they were no longer working from the registered address and had not been for 5 months prior to our inspection. The provider had failed to notify the commission of this change. The provider told us they did not have a new address as they were ‘working things out’. The provider failed to understand their legal requirements as a registered manager and provider.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not focus on continuous learning, innovation and improvement across the organisation and local system. Staff and leaders did not have a good understanding of how to make improvements happen. The provider told us they were aware of the areas that needed improving, however that had not taken any action to address the issues they identified. For example, the provider told us they were aware of the concerns around medicine administration records, however they had not taken action to ensure the records were competed accurately.

The provider failed to research and implement recognised guidance for people. The provider had not followed the principles of Right support, right care, right culture (RSRCRC). The RSRCRC outlines that we expect health and social care providers to guarantee autistic people and people with a learning disability the choices, dignity, independence and good access to local communities that most people take for granted. For example, care plans did not detail or document clearly people’s choices around their care and support or their capacity to make choices.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not understand their duty to collaborate and work in partnership, so services work seamlessly for people. They did not share information and learning with partners or collaborate for improvement. For example, the provider was not clear on what level of support had been assessed for people by the local authorities. The provider could not demonstrate they had been proactive to contact other health professionals in relation to people’s health needs for example for people with epilepsy.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not have a shared vision, strategy and culture based on transparency, equity, equality and human rights, diversity and inclusion, and engagement. They did not understand the challenges and the needs of people and their communities. The provider did not have effective systems to review the care people received, for example people’s care plans were very basic and lacked important information.

The provider had not identified the risks of a closed culture within the service. A "closed culture" is a poor culture that can lead to harm, including human rights breaches and abuse. We found a poor culture across the entire service, which had not been recognised or addressed by the provider. For example, the provider told us that staff sorted out breaks and rotas themselves, there was no oversight from the provider to ensure people were being supported by staff who were well rested and that staff’s wellbeing was considered and supported.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not value diversity in their workforce. They did not work towards an inclusive and fair culture by improving equality and equity for people who worked for them. The provider failed to ensure they had oversight of staff working hours. The provider told us they did not get involved with the rotas and that staff sorted the shifts out themselves. We found that staff were working for 72 hours without any recorded breaks which posed a risk to people and to staff. The provider had not ensured that the workforce was supported.

The provider could not demonstrate they had effective supervision processes in place. Whilst the provider told us they had identified concerns relating to staff, they had not carried out and documented supervisions to ensure the concerns were addressed and that staff had the support and opportunity to discuss where improvements were needed.
