asgRatings.title: Ongoing Assessment for Qualified Care Ltd
asgRatings.name: Homecare
asgRatings.commentary:
Date of assessment: 22 to 25 July 2025. Qualified Care Ltd is a domiciliary care agency providing personal care and support to people in their own homes. At the time of our inspection the service was providing personal care to 3 people. This was the first inspection of the service which was registered with CQC in December 2021.

We found significant shortfalls in the standard of care being delivered. The provider told us they did not have time to adequately monitor how the service was operating, and as a result had not identified that people were being exposed to a significant risk of harm. Where people had health conditions there was no or very little information for staff on how to support people with these, and where incidents of harm occurred the service was not taking any learning to prevent them from happening again. Staff were working extremely long periods of up to 20 hours a day for up to 10 days in a row without a break, putting both themselves and people they supported at risk of harm. People’s care needs had not been thoroughly assessed to ensure the service was able to safely support people, and staff were not trained in the needs of people they supported. Recruitment processes did not ensure staff were competent and safe to work with vulnerable people. There were large gaps in records where people had received care, but no information was documented or was only completed a significant amount of time later. The provider had no mechanisms to understand what care what being delivered. lacked knowledge about how the service was operating, and did not know the health and care needs of the people they supported.

The service was in breach of 6 legal requirements in relation to person centred care, safe care and treatment, safeguarding service users from abuse and improper treatment, good governance, staffing and failure to submit notifications of incidents.

This service is being placed in special measures. The purpose of special measures is to ensure that services providing inadequate care make significant improvements. Special measures provide a framework within which we use our enforcement powers in response to inadequate care and provide a timeframe within which providers must improve the quality of the care they provide. In instances where CQC have decided to take civil or criminal enforcement action against a provider, we will publish this information on our website after any representations and/ or appeals have been concluded.
asgRatings.narrative: The service is performing badly and we've taken action against the person or organisation that runs it.
asgRatings.overallPeopleExperience: Relatives we spoke to shared positive feedback on the service. However, we found that the service was putting people at a significant risk of harm, as staff were not trained or had sufficient information to be able to manage people’s health and care needs. The risks to people were not managed or assessed to ensure the service could safely care for them. Concerns had been raised by staff that they were working extremely long hours and were exhausted, but these had not been responded to. Management had a lack of awareness of how the service was operating and were oblivious to the extreme risks that people had been placed at as a result.

keyQuestionRatings.name: Caring
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Caring – this means we looked for evidence that the provider involved people and treated them with compassion, kindness, dignity and respect. This is the first assessment for this service. This key question has been rated Inadequate. This meant people were not treated with compassion and there were breaches of dignity; staff caring attitudes had significant shortfalls.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to treating people with dignity and respect.

topicareas.name: Independence, choice and control

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not always promote people’s independence, so people did not know their rights and have choice and control over their own care, treatment and wellbeing. People were not actively involved in their own care or treatment, or that of loved ones. We saw some examples of the provider working with people to enable them to have independence over elements of their care, for example one person had stated they wanted to administer medication themselves rather than staff. The service documented this conversation and updated their care arrangements accordingly. For another person a relative stated, “Staff support my relative in playing scrabble which means a lot to them and something they can participate with independently.” However, there was generally little consideration when planning people’s care as to how this could maximise people’s independence. Some people had restrictions put on them without the provider thoroughly assessing this as being in their best interests, and there was no guidance for staff for where intimate tasks were taking place how to ensure their wishes and preferences were respected.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Kindness, compassion and dignity

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not treat people with kindness, empathy and compassion, or respect their privacy and dignity. Relatives we spoke to stated staff were caring and compassionate. One relative told us, “Yes staff are cheerful and polite, they usually arrive on time and will tell us if running late. They communicate with my relative in a way that is compassionate, and that they can understand.” However, despite the praise for staff, we found people were not being treated with kindness because the service and staff did not have any knowledge of their unique health and care needs. If people’s health needs deteriorated, we could not be assured staff would know how to recognise this, how to respond and when they may need to request additional support from other services. People were being placed at a high risk of harm through the lack of oversight and governance at the service, and through being provided with staffing that was extremely unsafe.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Responding to people’s immediate needs

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not listen to or understand people’s needs, views and wishes. Staff did not respond to people’s needs in the moment or act to minimise any discomfort, concern or distress. There was very little guidance for staff on how to respond to people’s needs in a timely or safe manner. Staff explained multiple people often displayed extremely distressed behaviour, but there was no guidance on how staff should offer support, and people’s anxiety or distress was not being monitored to determine if there were any further steps staff could take to minimise this. Staffing levels and practices did not always allow staff to respond in a timely manner. We observed records of a staff member supporting one person who was extremely distressed, which meant they were unable to support another person at the same premises who also needed assistance at the same time. This person subsequently had an unwitnessed fall and had been placed at risk by the staffing levels in place.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Treating people as individuals

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not treat people as individuals or make sure people’s care, support and treatment met people’s needs and preferences. The provider did not take account of people’s strengths, abilities, aspirations, culture and unique backgrounds and protected characteristics. The was very little information about people detailed in their care plans, meaning the service had not given consideration to what may be important to the people they supported, how to ensure their preferences were being respected or that where people had things they wished to achieve that the staff could support them in doing so. The majority of people being supported lived with their families; however this was not mentioned in their care plans at all. Where personal care was being given, there was no guidance for staff on how to ensure this was being done in line with their preferences. For example, for one person it stated they needed equipment to help them shower and assistance from staff, however there was no detail on what this equipment was or how they may wish staff to support them to ensure their dignity and privacy was maximised. For another person their care plan stated staff would help them shower or wash, but staff stated, “No- we will rarely do this as they don’t like us to. But sometimes we will wash their back and help dry them.” However, this was not detailed in their care plan. We found that intimate tasks were being performed without appropriate guidance for staff, to ensure people were being actively involved and their wishes and preferences respected.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce wellbeing and enablement

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not care about or promote the wellbeing of their staff. They did not support or enable staff to deliver person-centred care. We found the provider had placed staff at an extreme risk of harm by expecting them to work for up to 20 hours a day, often without breaks for periods of up to 10 days at a time. They had failed in their duty of care towards their staff, and staff we spoke with described the physical and emotional impact this had on them. One staff member told us, “I am often awake all day and night as the people I support can be very distressed and need assistance. I have told the management that I am extremely tried and do not often get breaks. They do call and check how I am but nothing has been done.” When challenged on this the provider stated they did not know the hours they were expecting staff to work were unsafe.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Effective
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Effective – this means we looked for evidence that people’s care, treatment and support achieved good outcomes and promoted a good quality of life, based on best available evidence. This is the first assessment for this service. This key question has been rated Inadequate. This meant there were widespread and significant shortfalls in people’s care, support and outcomes.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to person centred care and safe care and treatment.

topicareas.name: Assessing needs

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not make sure people’s care and treatment was effective because they did not check and discuss people’s health, care, wellbeing and communication needs with them. The provider had failed to conduct comprehensive assessments to understand if they could support people prior to accepting new packages of care safely, or that they had continued to assess peoples need as they changed to ensure staff were supporting people appropriately. All the care plans we reviewed had very limited or no information about people’s health needs, or evidence the provider had any knowledge of these. For 1 person who the service had started supporting the manager told us, “They have dementia but I don’t know if they have any other health needs, we haven’t discussed this.” Staff told us one person’s needs had significantly increased in recent months, including a deterioration of their dementia, often becoming distressed. They said, “Now we have to support with medication, and sometimes assist them with personal care.” However, the manager had no knowledge that this was taking place, and their care plan had not been updated so did not reflect that the registered manager had considered how they could safely manage these needs.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Consent to care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not tell people about their rights around consent or respect these when delivering care and treatment. None of the staff working at the service had completed training on the Mental Capacity Act 2005. Therefore, the provider could not be assured they were aware of their responsibilities to support people in line with consent, and ensuring people were able to have capacity to make decisions for themselves unless assessed otherwise. Though care records recorded staff asking for consent, because staff had not received any training the provider could not be assured how this was being done or that staff had a clear understanding of how to do this in line with the law. One person had a restriction placed on them where medicines had been locked away by care staff, however there was no evidence of why this decision had been made, who had been involved and how the provider had assessed this decision was in a person’s best interests. There were discussions with people around how staff would support them in line with their mental capacity once they started using the service, but there was no evidence people’s mental capacity had been proactively reviewed after this point.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Delivering evidence-based care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not plan and deliver people’s care and treatment with them. They did not follow legislation and current evidence-based good practice and standards. There was very little information for staff explaining how they could support people’s health needs in line with clinical guidance or best practice. This included for conditions including falls, constipation, diabetes, mobility and dementia. Where people were distressed, there was antipsychotic medication in place which could be given to assist them when required. However there was no guidance on when this might be required, why medication was being given or if it was being given, if it was being effective. We could not be assured if staff were ensuring they were acting in the least restrictive manner possible and only using this medication where it was safe and necessary to do so.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: How staff, teams and services work together

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not work well across teams and services to support people. Staff we spoke to explained they were exhausted, and sometimes struggled to respond in a timely way to people’s need due to the lengthy hours they were working. Though we received positive comments about individual staff, they did not receive the support they required from the registered manager to provide safe care or treatment. Staff had no clear guidance on how they should work with other agencies involved in people’s care as well as their families. The provider explained to us how for some people they also had family members who would support in their care, but this was not mentioned at all in their care plans meaning there was a lack of clarity on who would be responsible for which tasks. One person had another care agency visiting them, but there was no detail of who this care agency were and how and when the provider may need to engage or work collaboratively with them to support this person’s needs.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Monitoring and improving outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not routinely monitor people’s care and treatment to continuously improve it. They did not ensure that outcomes were positive and consistent, or that they met both clinical expectations and the expectations of people themselves. The provider had no systems in place to monitor the care being delivered to ensure it was effective and supporting people to stay healthy and well. Multiple people were receiving “as and when” medicines which were to manage people’s constipation, anxiety and pain. Where they were being given, the provider failed to keep any records of why it had been given and if it had been effective. This meant they could not monitor if medicines were effectively managing people’s health needs, or if further medical advice may be needed to help people manage their condition. For people at risk of constipation staff explained, “We rely on the person telling us if they are in pain, then we can administer laxatives.” However this person had advanced dementia so we could not be assured they would be able to verbalise this, meaning they were at greater risk of harm as staff could not effectively monitor when they had gone to the toilet. Bowel charts were in place for this person but were not being filled in. There was often no written information on what care people should be receiving, and people’s care notes were often left blank or completed up to 5 days afterwards. Therefore, the provider had no ability to monitor if people were receiving the care they needed.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Supporting people to live healthier lives

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not support people to manage their health and wellbeing, so people could not maximise their independence, choice and control. Staff did not support people to live healthier lives, or where possible, reduce their future needs for care and support. There was no guidance on how staff should support people with their health needs to stay healthy and well. For most health conditions there was no detail about these in people’s care plan. For example, one person had a significant heart condition but this was not referenced in their care plan at all, so staff did not have any information on how to avoid exacerbating this. Another person had a wound on their leg which the care plan stated was being supported by visits from district nurses. However, staff told us this had not taken place for several months and the care plan had not been updated. Staff explained how they would apply creams and the symptoms of concern they would look out for. But there was no guidance to allow us to confirm what care this person should be receiving, or how staff were supporting this person to maintain healthy skin. Staff had received no training in the majority of the health conditions of the people they supported.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Responsive
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Responsive – this means we looked for evidence that the provider met people’s needs. This is the first assessment for this service. This key question has been rated Inadequate. This meant services were not planned or delivered in ways that met people’s needs. The provider did not plan or provide care that reflected people’s needs or considered factors that may result in inequity of access or experience of care.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to person centred care.

topicareas.name: Care provision, Integration and continuity

evidenceCategory.commentary: There were significant shortfalls in how the provider understood the diverse health and care needs of people and their local communities, so care was not joined-up, flexible or supportive of choice and continuity. There was no joined up approach to care by the staff that were working at the service. Staff were not always completing the daily care notes with detail of what care had been given.Therefore, we were concerned about how a new member of staff coming in the next day would understand any concerns arising from previous days. A relative stated they had a consistent staff team working with them, however they were not working safe hours and lacked any detailed information on how to safely support people.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in access

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not make sure that people could access the care, support and treatment they needed when they needed it. The provider did not understand the diverse health and care needs of the people they supported, how they should be met and at what point they may need additional support from other agencies. Staff were not suitably trained or provided with sufficient information to be able understand what care and treatment people needed, or how to provide it.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in experiences and outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary: Staff and leaders did not listen to information about people who are most likely to experience inequality in experience or outcomes. This meant people’s care was not tailored in response to this. All the people being supported by the service were living with dementia, but the provider was not aware of this and had not put in place any detailed guidance on how that presented for each person, and any adjustments that may need to be put in place so they could fully engage with their care. One person had a hearing impairment as well as dementia, but their care plan simply stated that they had these conditions without giving any consideration to what this meant for their care, or how those two conditions may interact and affect this person and how they perceived the world or experience of care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Listening to and involving people

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not make it easy for people to share feedback and ideas, or raise complaints about their care, treatment and support. Staff did not always involve people in decisions about their care or tell them what had changed as a result. Relatives we spoke with explained they received regular surveys to ask for their feedback, and felt comfortable in raising a complaint to management if needed. One relative told us, “I’ve never had a cause for complaint, but would be confident in how to do so if needed.” However people’s care plans were outdated, and we could only see limited evidence that the provider was continually involving people in reviewing their care, to ensure that they were receiving care that met their needs and preferences. For instance, one person’s care plan stated they had not had a fall, when they had fallen several times. But there was no evidence of the provider reviewing the care plan with this person or their representatives as a result.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Person-centred Care

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not make sure people were at the centre of their care and treatment choices and they did not work in partnership with people, to decide how to respond to any relevant changes in people’s needs. People’s care plans did not reflect people as a whole including their health and care needs, life histories or diverse backgrounds. There was no clear detail set out on what people’s needs were, how the service should meet these and how this had been discussed in partnership with people. Where people’s health needs had changed, the care plans had not been updated so did not reflect the needs of people as they currently were. For example one person had diabetes and although staff supported this person with nutrition and hydration, there was no guidance on how this would be managed safely to avoid exacerbating their condition. There was no mention of this person has having diabetes in their care plan at all, beyond in a list of medications.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Planning for the future

evidenceCategory.commentary: People were not supported to plan for important life changes, so they could have enough time to make informed decisions about their future, including at the end of their life. There was no information recorded about people’s wishes for the future, and how the registered manager had explored these with people or any support they could provide in ensuring they took place. For example, there was no recorded information for people’s wishes for end of life or evidence that the provider had discussed these with people.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Providing Information

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not supply appropriate, accurate and up-to-date information in formats that were tailored to individual needs. Relatives we spoke with felt that staff communicated with people in an inclusive way that allowed them to participate in their care. One relative told us, “(Relative name) is profoundly deaf, but staff communicate with them using a whiteboard and gestures to help them communicate which works well.” However, detailed information was not always recorded of the care that was being delivered and the provider had failed to maintain up to date records. The care notes that were being maintained lacked detail and were often not being completed at all, meaning relatives or people wishing to view these would not be able to have a record of the care actually being delivered. The provider had failed to ensure where they were holding sensitive information on people’s health and care needs, that this was up to date and comprehensive. For example where people’s needs had changed including around deterioration of health conditions, this was not detailed in their care plans which had not been updated. The provider was also not recording the hours staff were working, so we could not be assured people’s consumer rights were being upheld and that the provider was charging people for the actual amount of care being delivered.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Safe
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Safe – this means we looked for evidence that people were protected from abuse and avoidable harm. This is the first assessment for this service. This key question has been rated Inadequate. This meant people were not safe and were at risk of avoidable harm.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to safe care and treatment, staffing and safeguarding service users from abuse and improper treatment.

topicareas.name: Infection prevention and control

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not always assess or manage the risk of infection. Staff had received training in infection prevention and a staff member explained to us, “Yes when doing personal care I would always wear, gloves, masks and aprons. There are always enough supplies of these for us.” However, the provider could not evidence they had undertaken any checks to confirm if staff were following appropriate protocols for preventing infections in practice.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Involving people to manage risks

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not work well with people to understand and manage risks. Staff did not provide care to meet people’s needs that was safe, supportive and enabled people to do the things that mattered to them. Where people had health conditions, there was no guidance or information for staff on how to help people manage these safely. For example all the people being supported were at risk of falls, but there was no guidance for staff on how to prevent people from falling or how to respond safely when people did fall. One person had recently suffered a fall who was receiving anti-clotting medicine which means a significantly increased risk of internal bleeding, yet staff did not request medical advice from 999 or 111 following the fall to ensure the persons wellbeing and to receive any necessary treatment. There was no guidance for staff explaining the risks around anti-clotting medicines. Once we raised concerns to the provider, risk assessments were put in place however these were not personalised to the people receiving care and continued to lack detail on how they would be safely supported. This included a person living with diabetes where there was no information on what their normal blood sugar levels were, or what staff should do if the person’s diabetes caused them to become unwell. We were concerned that staff would not be able to recognise symptoms or concerns or understand when they may need to request medical advice if this person’s health deteriorated.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning culture

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not have a proactive and positive culture of safety based on openness and honesty. They did not listen to concerns about safety and did not investigate or report safety events. Lessons were not learnt to continually identify and embed good practice. Where incidents took place, the provider had failed to analyse them or take learning to prevent the incident from reoccurring. For a person who had regularly fallen, incident reports did not contain any detail on potential causes of the falls, or any steps the provider had taken to support the persons mobility and prevent the future risk of falling. Despite these falls, the provider had failed to ensure there was adequate guidance or risk assessment in place to enable staff to support this person safely. Staff meetings and supervisions were taking place which did discuss the risks to the people being supported, but despite this the provider had failed to identify that staff lacked the training or guidance to safely support people and protect them from harm.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Medicines optimisation

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not always make sure that medicines and treatments were safe and met people’s needs, capacities and preferences. We were told that staff supported 2 people to receive their medicines, but the provider had failed to ensure they received any training in how to do this and had not assessed whether staff were competent to do so. This included staff administering controlled drugs. There were significant gaps in people’s records, including days where staff had not recorded if medicine had been given or not. Where “as and when” medicine was in place, there was no guidance on when these should be given and staff had not recorded why it was being administered or whether it had been effective or not. One person had a controlled drug pain patch in place which needed to be rotated across different parts of the body to reduce the risk of serious side effects, but there was no guidance on how to manage these safely or state where on the body these patches were being applied to.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe and effective staffing

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not make sure there were enough qualified, skilled and experienced staff. They did not always make sure staff received effective support, supervision and development. They did not work together well to provide safe care that met people’s individual needs. Staff we spoke with told us they were regularly working up to 20 hours a day, often without a break and for periods of up to 10 days consecutively. One staff member told us “Working here can be extremely difficult. I am only contracted to work in the day, but I have to work throughout the night also as the people I care for need extensive support. I am often very tired and have no energy to support them. I get breaks sometimes but not every day.” The provider told us they had no systems to allow them to track the number of hours staff were working. This meant people were being exposed to an extremely high risk of harm, as staff were working unsafe hours which reduced their ability to meet people’s needs in an effective manner. Staff were not trained or knowledgeable in how to manage the health needs of the people they supported, this included around mental health conditions, and health conditions including constipation, diabetes, falls risk and promoting healthy skin. We also identified staff were administering medicines without having had any training in this area, or the provider assessing that they were safe and competent to do so. The provider did not follow safe practices to ensure fit and proper staff were employed, which included DBS (Disclosure and Barring Service) and reference checks only being completed after staff had started working for the service. Where the provider’s family members had been employed, the provider had failed to ensure interviews or recruitment processes were impartial. For instance interviews were conducted by relatives, or references provided by companies we were informed were also owned by relatives.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe environments

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not always detect and control potential risks in the care environment. They did not always make sure equipment, facilities and technology supported the delivery of safe care.Although the provider could demonstrate they had assessed the environmental risks in people’s private houses both to people and staff, they had not set out clear guidance of how these risks would be safely managed. For example the risk assessment identified that stairs posed a risk to one person due to their poor mobility, but there was no information about how this would be managed. Though the provider told us they conducted spot visits of people’s houses to ensure they had an up to date picture of any risks posed to people, they could not provide any documentation evidencing this had taken place meaning we could not be assured they had an accurate overview of how safe the environments they were working in were.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe systems, pathways and transitions

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not work well with people and health system partners to establish and maintain safe systems of care. They did not manage or monitor people’s safety. They did not make sure there was continuity of care, including when people moved between different services. Where the service started supporting new people, they failed to conduct a robust assessment of their needs which meant they were unaware of the majority of people’s health conditions and how to safely care for them. This meant the service and staff were not ensuring people transitioned to the service safely, or aware of their responsibility to work in collaboration with other health and care services where appropriate. One person was at risk of diabetes but there was no guidance at all on how this should be managed safely, when to recognise concerns or who they would refer to and at what point to ensure this person received the support they needed. Another person was at risk of falls and the manager told us, “We work with a local falls response team who can assist us if (person name) has a fall and needs support in standing.” However, there was no reference at all to this team in their care plan, meaning staff did not have any clear guidance on how to contact them when needed meaning this person risked being in an undignified and uncomfortable position for longer if they fell.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safeguarding

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not work well with people and healthcare partners to understand what being safe meant to them and how to achieve that. They did not concentrate on improving people’s lives or protecting their right to live in safety, free from bullying, harassment, abuse, discrimination, avoidable harm and neglect. The provider did not share concerns quickly and appropriately. The service was not protecting people’s right to live in safety because they did not understand the risks to people, and staff did not have a clear understanding or information on how support people safely or support them in having the best quality of life possible. The registered manager told us, “Where people have fallen, we have been told not to report this as a safeguarding if there were no injuries.” However, they had failed to recognise that people could still be being neglected or receiving poor quality of care even this did not result in an injury, and had not notified any statutory bodies, which they are legally required to do, when people had fallen.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Well-led – this means we looked for evidence that service leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation; and promoted an open, fair culture. This is the first assessment for this service. This key question has been rated Inadequate. This meant there were widespread and significant shortfalls in leadership. Leaders and the culture they created did not assure the delivery of high-quality care.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to good governance and failure to submit notifications of incidents.

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not have inclusive leaders at all levels who understood the context in which they delivered care, treatment and support, or who embodied the culture and values of their workforce and organisation. Leaders did not have the skills, knowledge, experience and credibility to lead effectively, and they did not do so with integrity, openness and honesty. The provider told us they did not have any systems in place to monitor how many hours staff were working, however staff told us they had raised their concerns about the unsafe nature of the hours they were expected to work. Management had failed in their duty of care to their staff and to people being supported, as staff were working hours that did not allow them to operate safely. The provider was not fully aware of their responsibilities to ensure risks to people were being safely managed, and did not put in place risk assessments for how to manage people’s health needs until after we conducted our inspection.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary: People did not always feel they could speak up and that their voice would be heard. Staff explained to us they knew how to speak up, with one staff member telling us, “Yes if I have any concerns I would speak to the manager or deputy. I am comfortable in doing this, and there are regular meetings and supervision sessions”. There was a policy in place detailing other organisations staff could approach to share any concerns. However, where staff had raised concerns about unsafe working practices, these had not been addressed meaning where concerns were raised action had not always been taken to ensure people were safe or that staff were listened to.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not have clear responsibilities, roles, systems of accountability and good governance. They did not act on the best information about risk, performance and outcomes, or share this securely with others when appropriate. Both the manager and deputy manager at the service told us they had other full-time employment, which meant they did not have the time to effectively manage the service or monitor the quality of care being delivered. We were told some audits of medication and spot visits had been conducted, but no evidence of these could be provided. The systems in place had not identified that risks to people’s health were being poorly managed and had placed them at risk of significant harm, and the care documentation we reviewed was outdated and lacked sufficient detail. For one person although they had received care visits every day in July up to the date of our inspection, there were only records completed for 3 days. Therefore, the provider had no knowledge of what care had been delivered on the other days. Despite this having been discussed as a concern at staff meeting in June, the records of care being delivered were often still not being completed or only completed several days later. We were told this was because some staff had other employment and did not have time to complete these, which the provider had failed to address. When we discussed the people being supported, management were not aware of what care was actually being provided due to their lack of appropriate monitoring systems.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not focus on continuous learning, innovation and improvement across the organisation and local system. They did not encourage creative ways of delivering equality of experience, outcome and quality of life for people. Where incidents had occurred, there was no learning taken from these to identify why they may have occurred and any changes the provider could make going forward. Despite multiple people having had recent falls, their care plans were not updated to reflect people’s current needs and how to prevent and respond to them. Staff we spoke with were uncertain about their responsibilities with one staff member saying, “No it isn’t our responsibility to assist somebody up after a fall. We would wait for the ambulance.” But despite this staff were documented as helping people to raise from the floor after a fall. The governance systems in place had not identified the lack of clarity for staff despite multiple opportunities where this could have been identified. The provider could not share evidence of any audits or monitoring they told us they had completed or tell us about improvements they had made as a result.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not understand their duty to collaborate and work in partnership, so services work seamlessly for people. They did not share information and learning with partners or collaborate for improvement. People’s care plans contained little detail of any other agencies involved in their care, and how staff should work alongside them to support people’s health needs and to live the best possible quality of life. For example, where people had conditions including dementia, constipation, diabetes, wounds, limited mobility, heart conditions or were at risk of falls there was no guidance for staff to support them around signs and symptoms to look out for, and when they should escalate these to other organisations for advice and support. Where medication was prescribed for people by professionals, staff were not given guidance to ensure this was being safely administered or monitored to allow these to be given as prescribed. Where incidents had occurred, they had not followed their statutory duty to notify the CQC.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not have a shared vision, strategy and culture based on transparency, equity, equality and human rights, diversity and inclusion, and engagement. The provider did not respect the human rights of the people, or of their staff. People were being given care and treatment that was unsafe and had not considered their health or social needs. They had failed to identify that some restrictions on people had been made without appropriately assessing if this was in their best interests, or that anti-psychotic medications were being given in a way that also acted as a chemical restraint as the grounds for their usage were not clearly stated or effectiveness monitored.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not value diversity in their workforce. They did not work towards an inclusive and fair culture by improving equality and equity for people who worked for them. We saw no evidence demonstrating how the provider has considered the diverse needs of their workforce and how they could support them. There was no evidence of how they had considered any adaptations needed to ensure their staff were safe, and had exposed them to extremely unsafe working hours and expected them to provide care with little information on how to safely support people’s needs.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care
