topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Safe
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Safe – this means we looked for evidence that people were protected from abuse and avoidable harm. At our last assessment we rated this key question inadequate. At this assessment the rating has remained inadequate. This meant people were not safe and were at risk of avoidable harm.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to safe care and treatment, the way people’s medicines were managed safely and staffing.

topicareas.name: Infection prevention and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider assessed and managed the risk of infection. They detected and controlled the risk of it spreading and shared concerns with appropriate agencies promptly.

People did not raise concerns about infection prevention practices. Staff understood what personal protection equipment was required to minimise the risks to people. The provider supplied staff with personal protection equipment to undertake their roles.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Involving people to manage risks

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not work well with people to understand and manage risks. Staff did not provide care to meet people’s needs that was safe, supportive and enabled people to do the things that mattered to them.

At our previous inspection we found processes to assess, record and mitigate risks to people were inadequate. This remained the case at this inspection and people were not protected from the risk of harm. People’s risk assessment and care plan guidance remained unclear and missed important information. One person who used a wheelchair had no risk assessment for this although staff confirmed the person used one within their daily notes. Another person had been injured by their wheelchair but following this incident their care plan had not been updated to reflect this was a risk. When we asked the provider about it, they said, “It’s an eye opener I’m being asked to do a risk assessment for the wheelchair, thank you for bringing that up.”

Another person had sustained a fall and bruised their shoulder. The provider had not updated the person’s risk assessment or care plan accordingly. Where the provider had risk assessed some people were at risk of falling, they had not ensured risk assessments were robust, for example 1 people was on a medicine which could increase their risk of falling which had not been considered as part of their assessment. The provider had not risk assessed according to people’s individual needs. For example, people used various equipment such as pressure relieving cushions, bed levers and foot stools, all of which had not been included in risk assessments or care plan guidance.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not have a proactive and positive culture of safety based on openness and honesty. They did not listen to concerns about safety and did not investigate or report safety events. Lessons were not learnt to continually identify and embed good practice.

At our previous inspection we found the provider did not learn from safety incidents, events and findings from checks and audits. This continued to be the case, the provider had failed to take appropriate action in response to events and there was no learning to prevent people from being further harmed. Although some action and been documented after incidents the provider failed to maintain a good oversight and it was not clear if appropriate action had always been taken. For example, following a person falling it was not clear if the appropriate health care professionals have been contacted. Risk assessments following incidents and accidents were not updated which meant people’s care records continued to lack crucial information for staff to support them safely.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Medicines optimisation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not make sure that medicines and treatments were safe and met people’s needs, capacities and preferences. People were not involved in planning.

At our previous inspection we found concerns with home medicines nor being managed which put people at risk of harm. At this inspection we found continued concerns with the management of medicines. We found gaps in medicine records and concerns with how people received their medicines which were not clearly explained by the provider. We identified concerns with a person’s medicines and was not assured they received their medicine as prescribed. The provider told us the person’s family would put their medicines in a Dossett box; however, the provider then sent us information which started the person had blister packs for their medicines and the issue was around recording. The person’s medicine records had not been updated to say their medicines were administered from blister packs. The provider’s audits and checks had not identified the concerns we identified.

At our previous inspection we found Medicine Administration Record (MAR) charts were not completed as recommended in the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines and this continued to be the case at this inspection, codes were still being used rather than staff initials. People prescribed high risk medicines were not assessed. For example, a person was prescribed an anticoagulant. This medicine can increase the risk of falling. There was no risk assessment in place for this or guidance for staff to refer to in the event of a fall or injury. A person was prescribed an anti-seizure medicine; this had not been identified or considered by the provider and no risk assessment was in place should they experience seizures whilst on anticoagulants.

Another person was prescribed pain relieving patches which should be rotated on the body when re-administered. The person’s record within their home for April 2025 had not been properly recorded so it was not clear if they have received this medicine safely. The provider had a poor oversight of people’s medicines and told us they did not know what medicines 2 people were prescribed because the 2 people did not want to tell them. When we spoke to the 2 people, they were very happy to share what medicines they were prescribed, and this was not an issue for them. We had raised concerns with the provider at the previous inspection about them not knowing what medicines people were administered and the impact of them not understanding what side effects people could experience which could cause risks to their safety, such at them being more prone to falling. The provider had a complete lack of oversight about their responsibly around managing risks and they failed to implement strategies to reduce the risk of harm where possible.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe and effective staffing

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not make sure there were enough qualified, skilled and experienced staff. They did not always make sure staff received effective support, supervision and development. They did not work together well to provide safe care that met people’s individual needs.

At our previous inspection we identified concerns around the deployment of staff and the training staff received. This continued to be a concern at this inspection. The provider lacked any oversight of calls times which often ran late or were cut short, some as short as 4 minutes long. The provider could give no clear or appropriate rationale for this and stated people did not mind. The provider told us their policy stated there was a half an hour ‘leeway’ either side for calls to not be on time but provided no policy to back up this statement. Some people we spoke to were unaware how long their call should be.

The providers training matrix provided no assurance that staff were up to date with their learning and development or they had the right skills and competence to support people safely. The training matrix indicated multiple topics of training were competed within a small window of time. There were no assurances of certificates or accreditation to assess the quality of the training staff received. Moving and handling training was conducted online, with no evidence of practical training received by staff who were supporting people who required equipment to assist them to transfer. The provider’s competency assessments did not detail observations made or staff understanding of their training. There was no evidence any supervisions or appraisals had happened this year.

Some appropriate checks had been completed prior to staff starting work which included checks through the Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS). DBS checks provide information including details about convictions and cautions held on the Police National Computer. The information helps employers make safer recruitment decisions. However, we found concerns with other checks the provider made. The provider told us they did not retain interview notes and only formally interviewed older individuals and would informally interview younger candidates. The provider said if a potential new staff member was an overseas candidate they would be more thorough but a potential staff member who was not from overseas would have been employed by other organisations so they would not need to be as thorough. We fed back out concerns to the provider about this approach who said, “We do have set questions, but I don’t record discussion. I perfectly understand if someone said they didn't like babies then applied to work in a school it would be a concern but going forward if we take on new staff I would definitely think about making it more formal”.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe environments

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always detect and control potential risks in the care environment. They did not make sure that equipment, facilities and technology supported the delivery of safe care.

At our last inspection we found there was a failure to adequately assess people’s environments so that care could be delivered in a safe way. We found this was a continued concern at this inspection. People’s care files continued to contain generic risk assessments about ensuring their environment was safe and were almost identical containing the same information. We visited 3 people in their homes and observed they used specific equipment to support their mobility and other individual needs which had not been robustly risk assessed or considered by the provider in a personalised way. One person had their bed against a radiator, but no risk assessment had been implemented by the provider.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe systems, pathways and transitions

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not work well with people and health system partners to establish and maintain safe systems of care. They did not manage or monitor people’s safety. They did not make sure there was continuity of care, including when people moved between different services

At the previous inspection we found there was a complete lack of awareness of risks and safety across people’s care journey, and this placed people at risk of significant harm. This continued to be the case at this inspection. The provider had a poor oversight of the individual needs of people. They were not aware what medicine some people took or if people had skin integrity concerns.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safeguarding

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not work well with people and healthcare partners to understand what being safe meant to them and how to achieve that. They did not concentrate on improving people’s lives or protecting their right to live in safety, free from bullying, harassment, abuse, discrimination, avoidable harm and neglect. The provider did not share concerns quickly and appropriately.

At our previous inspection we found safeguarding systems were inadequate and people were not protected from harm. The provider told us at this inspection there had been no safeguarding concerns since the previous inspection which would require escalation to the local authority. However, we remained concerned safeguarding concerns would not be safely managed. The providers safeguarding policy had not been updated since October 2023 and stated this should be reviewed annually or sooner. The policy named a staff member as the safeguarding lead but provided no details of what their position was or how they should be contacted. The policy gave contradictory information as it also indicated the individual worked for the local authority. The policy provided details for 2 separate local authorities which meant it would be unclear to staff as to which one should be contacted to report any safeguarding concerns.

When people had been harmed there was no evidence of meaningful action or learning. For example, a person told staff they had a sore on their bottom and the district nurse was visiting them. The provider was unaware about the person’s wound and had not risk assessed this or provided staff with any information about how to support the person to prevent the wound becoming worse. This further demonstrated a continued lack of oversight of the providers risk management.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Well-led – this means we looked for evidence that service leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation; and promoted an open, fair culture.

At our last assessment we rated this key question inadequate. At this assessment the rating has remained inadequate. This meant there were widespread and significant shortfalls in leadership. Leaders and the culture they created did not assure the delivery of high-quality care.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to governance at the service.

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not have inclusive leaders at all levels who understood the context in which they delivered care, treatment and support, or who embodied the culture and values of their workforce and organisation. Leaders did not have the skills, knowledge, experience and credibility to lead effectively, and they did not do so with integrity, openness and honesty.

The provider lacked knowledge of their responsibilities and of the regulations. They did not lead by example to promote an inclusive culture and failed to assess the quality-of-care people were receiving. The provider failed to ensure people received safe care and treatment and had not ensured staff were provided with the right training or information to support people well.

Throughout the inspection the provider was combative making statements such as, "Don’t put words in my mouth" and “That’s what im trying to explain to you". They were not forthcoming with the information we requested or accepting of our feedback about the concerns we found at times.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary:
People did not feel they could speak up and that their voice would be heard.

During the previous inspection, we received information that some staff were told not to speak with inspectors from CQC and only staff who were friends and family of the registered manager were permitted to speak with us. During this inspection we found this continued to be a concern. The provider did not always co-operate and attempted to encourage people not to meet us in person to allow them the opportunity to provide face to face feedback about their care and support. We asked to speak to the admin staff member, but the provider said they had to go as they had an appointment. We said we could phone them when convenient and the provider said, “They only do admin.” and appeared to be trying to put us off talking to them.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not have clear responsibilities, roles, systems of accountability and good governance. They did not act on the best information about risk, performance and outcomes, or share this securely with others when appropriate.

The provider’s oversight of the service continued to be poor. The service leadership oversight remained a concern. Audits of medicines did not highlight issues found at this inspection. The provider’s response to our findings regarding gaps on the day of our site visit differed from the information they sent after the onsite inspection. We were not assured documentation was an accurate or truthful reflection of the service. The provider’s spot checks did not focus on vital areas of care such as medicines and care records.

The provider was only supporting a small amount of people, but their audits had not identified where people's care records were not aligned with the actual care delivery. The provider lacked understanding about their regulatory responsibilities. They had moved their office location without informing the Commission or following the correct or expected process.

The registered manager’s registration with the Commission was cancelled in January 2025. The provider had not provided assurances of how the service was being managed or the plans to recruit to the position of registered manager. The provider confirmed after our site visit the interim management arrangements. However, we were not assured because the provider also confirmed the individual they said would be the interim manager was not employed which raised concerns regarding what checks had been made for them to oversee the service and access people's records.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not focus on continuous learning, innovation and improvement across the organisation and local system. They did not encourage creative ways of delivering equality of experience, outcome and quality of life for people. They did not actively contribute to safe, effective practice and research.

The leadership of the service continued to be poor, and the provider did not demonstrate a good understanding of how improvements needed to be implemented. We found continued breaches of regulation at this inspection and people continued to be at risk of harm and poor care. The provider continued to lack understanding that assessment and management of all risks to people they supported should be considered and incorporated into their support plans and assessments. We remained concerned there was a closed culture at the service and the provider did not demonstrate they were open to learning or understood the importance of continuous improvement.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not understand their duty to collaborate and work in partnership, so services work seamlessly for people. They did not share information and learning with partners or collaborate for improvement.

Only a small number of people received support from the provider since our previous inspection. Although a person told us they were visited by the district nurses to help them manage their health needs this was due to their own ability rather than the support of the provider to facilitate partnership working. We were not assured the provider always collaborated effectively and openly with relevant stakeholders and agencies to ensure that people were safe and received the support they needed. The provider’s records were poor and people continued to be at risk due to the absence of processes to support collaborative working with partners, including sharing information and improvement that could be made to people's support.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not have a shared vision, strategy and culture based on transparency, equity, equality and human rights, diversity and inclusion, and engagement. They did not understand the challenges and the needs of people and their communities.

The provider continued to not demonstrate a positive culture. The provided told us one of their objectives was to make care as individualised as possible and they wanted to make sure care was personalised and they made sure staff had the right skills. We found concerns with the individual care of people and the training and supervision of staff. The provider could not demonstrate any sustained improvement since our previous inspection, and little had changed at the service to demonstrate people received a good service. The provider said they would give questionnaires for people to complete to get feedback about the service but had not done this for some time.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not value diversity in their workforce. They did not work towards an inclusive and fair culture by improving equality and equity for people who worked for them.

The provider did not provide any assurance they worked towards an inclusive culture. They provided no evidence around how they promoted people’s equity or equality.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

asgRatings.title: Ongoing Assessment for Best2 Care Ltd – Gravesend Office
asgRatings.name: Homecare
asgRatings.commentary:
We carried out this assessment between 22 June and 6 July 2026. Best2Care Ltd – Gravesend Office is a care at home agency that provides care and support to people with a range of physical health, mental health, learning disability and autism-related needs in their own homes. At the time of this assessment there were 8 people receiving support with ‘personal care’: which is help with tasks related to personal hygiene and eating. Not everyone using the service receives the regulated activity of personal care. Where they do, we also take into account any wider social care provided. We did not review people’s care and support who did not receive personal care.

At our last assessment published on 27 November 2021, the service was in breach of 3 regulations relating to person-centred care, safe recruitment and governance. At this assessment, the service had made improvements and was no longer in breach of any regulations.

We assessed the service against ‘Right support, right care, right culture’ guidance to make judgements about whether the provider guaranteed people with a learning disability and autistic people respect, equality, dignity, choices, independence and good access to local communities that most people take for granted.

The service promoted continuity and consistency in care delivery. People received care and support from regular team of care staff. There were sufficient staff deployed to support people.

People were safeguarded from abuse. People were supported to access healthcare services, maintain their wellbeing and remain involved in their local communities. Staff were trained to support people effectively. Staff followed infection prevention and control procedures. Incidents and accidents were reported and reviewed and lessons learned from them.

People and relatives were involved in assessments, reviews and decisions about their care. Care plans detailed people's individual needs, risks, and how these would be met. Staff supported people in a way that promoted their independence, choice and control.

The provider had systems in place to monitor quality and safety, including audits of care records, medicines, incidents, complaints and call monitoring. Leaders were approachable, and staff felt well supported through supervision, training and ongoing development opportunities. The provider also worked with an external compliance organisation and sector networks to support continuous improvement.
asgRatings.narrative: The service is performing well and meeting our expectations.
asgRatings.overallPeopleExperience:
People and their relatives were positive about their experiences of receiving care from Best2Care Ltd – Gravesend Office. They consistently described staff as kind, caring, reliable and respectful. People told us they felt safe with staff and valued receiving support from a small, regular team of carers who knew them well.

People said staff treated them with dignity and respect, listened to their views and involved them in decisions about their care. People told us staff promoted their independence and encouraged them to do as much as possible for themselves. They felt comfortable discussing their needs with staff and the registered manager and told us support was flexible and responsive when changes were needed. Relatives also spoke positively about staff's understanding of people's individual needs, routines and preferences and said staff adapted their approach accordingly.

People receiving support with mental health needs said staff provided both practical and emotional support, helping them to feel reassured and supported.

Relatives described staff as knowledgeable, patient and committed to achieving good outcomes for people.

People and relatives spoke highly of the registered manager, describing them as approachable, supportive and responsive. They told us communication was good and felt confident that any concerns or requests would be listened to and acted upon.

keyQuestionRatings.name: Caring
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Caring – this means we looked for evidence that the provider involved people and treated them with compassion, kindness, dignity and respect.

At our last assessment we rated this key question good. At this assessment the rating has remained good.

This meant people were supported and treated with dignity and respect; and involved as partners in their care.

topicareas.name: Independence, choice and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider promoted people’s independence, so people knew their rights and had choice and control over their own care, treatment and wellbeing.

People told us staff supported them to maintain their independence. A person said, “I am fully capable of speaking. I require support with my mobility. I strive to remain as independent as I can and do as much as I can.” Another person told us they were able to prepare their own meals and only requested support when they were unable to do so. Records also showed some people were supported to manage their own medicines, with a person's care plan confirming they were able to self-administer their medication.

Care plans emphasised the importance of promoting independence and encouraging people to maintain existing skills. Daily care records demonstrated how staff supported people to make choices, retain control over their care and participate in decisions about their daily lives.

Staff understood the importance of enabling people to remain independent and exercise choice. A staff member told us, “We get the clients involved because it’s about them. We provide choices and explain the benefits, but it is their right to choose what they want.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Kindness, compassion and dignity

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider always treated people with kindness, empathy and compassion and respected their privacy and dignity. Staff treated colleagues from other organisations with kindness and respect.

People and their relatives spoke positively about the caring approach of staff. A person told us, “I have a really good rapport with 1 of the carers who I am able to confide in, I trust them, they listen to me and understand.” A relative also commented that, “The carers are very respectful and helpful.”

Care plans highlighted the importance of treating people with dignity and respect and included guidance on providing person-centred support. Staff understood how to uphold people's privacy, dignity and independence in practice. A staff member told us, “Kindness and dignity also include how you speak to people. You must speak to people in a polite manner and listen to them. You also make sure you give them their space and support with personal care in a dignified way.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Responding to people’s immediate needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider listened to and understood people’s needs, views and wishes. Staff responded to people’s needs in the moment and acted to minimise any discomfort, concern or distress.

People and relatives told us staff were attentive, understanding and responsive to their individual needs. A person said, “If I am having a bad day the carers will do more to help me through it. They are very obliging and understanding.” Another person told us, “I trust them and they help me feel safe emotionally,” demonstrating the emotional support staff provided alongside practical care.

Relatives also spoke positively about staff's ability to recognise and respond to changing needs. A relative told us, “The carers do everything from washing to feeding, they are very vigilant and would act upon anything if necessary.” Another relative said staff understood their loved one’s needs and were patient, reliable and responsive to their routines and preferences.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Treating people as individuals

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider treated people as individuals and made sure people’s care, support and treatment met people’s needs and preferences. They took account of people’s strengths, abilities, aspirations, culture and unique backgrounds and protected characteristics.

People and their relatives told us staff provided personalised care and understood what was important to them. Care plans contained information about people's day-to-day support needs and how these should be met in a way that reflected individual preferences and routines. A relative told us, “The carers we have are very supportive and understand my loved one’s needs and how to handle and motivate them to co-operate, and it is working well.”

Relatives described how staff adapted their approach to meet individual needs and respected established routines that were important to people's wellbeing. For example, a relative explained staff followed their loved one's routine because consistency was important to them. Records also showed people's preferences were respected, including one person who preferred to receive personal care from staff of the same gender.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce wellbeing and enablement

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider cared about and promoted the wellbeing of their staff, and supported and enabled staff to always deliver person-centred care.

Staff told us they received regular supervision and ongoing support from the management team. A staff member said, “I get at least monthly supervision and more if I need to. The registered manager is someone I can talk to anytime. She has supported me in many ways to ensure I feel settled and able to do the job. She is a blessing to me.” Feedback discussed during supervisions demonstrated staff were encouraged to reflect on their practice and development needs.

The provider considered staff wellbeing when planning care delivery. Rotas were designed to incorporate days off, allow sufficient travel time between visits and, where possible, accommodate staff's personal circumstances for example staff worked around their family and other personal commitments. Staff told us they had regular contact from the registered manager which helped ensure they felt supported, particularly when working alone. A lone working policy was in place to promote staff safety.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Effective
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Effective – this means we looked for evidence that people’s care, treatment and support achieved good outcomes and promoted a good quality of life, based on best available evidence.

At our last assessment we rated this key question requires improvement. At this assessment the rating has changed to good.

This meant people’s outcomes were consistently good, and people’s feedback confirmed this.

topicareas.name: Assessing needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider made sure people’s care and treatment was effective by assessing and reviewing their health, care, wellbeing and communication needs with them.

People and their relatives told us they were involved in initial assessments and discussions about their care. Assessment processes considered people’s holistic needs, including their physical health, mental wellbeing, personal care requirements, communication needs, risks and support to access the community. This helped ensure care and support were tailored to people's individual needs, preferences and circumstances.

The provider worked collaboratively with healthcare and social care professionals to ensure people's needs were accurately assessed and reviewed. Where appropriate, joint assessments were undertaken with external professionals to ensure risks and support needs were fully considered. Staff also made referrals to specialist services, including mental health teams, when additional support or advice was required.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Consent to care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider told people about their rights around consent and respected these when delivering person-centred care and treatment.

People told us they were supported to make their own choices and remain independent. A person said, “I can make my own decisions; they guide me and encourage me to do what I can for myself.” This demonstrated staff promoted people's independence while providing support when needed.

The provider worked in line with the principles of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 (MCA). Mental capacity assessments had been completed where there were concerns about a person's ability to make specific decisions. Records showed decisions were made in people's best interests when appropriate and involved relevant people and professionals.

Staff received training on the Mental Capacity Act and understood the importance of supporting people to make their own decisions wherever possible. Relatives confirmed they were involved in decisions when appropriate. A relative told us, “I am fully involved in my loved one's care and changes and decisions would come through me. I will speak to the manager as they are aware of the situation.” Care records reflected decisions made about people's care and support. Staff had received MCA training. A staff member said, “We can't force anyone against their well. They have a right to refuse care or even their medication. We provide choice and explain benefits.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Delivering evidence-based care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider planned and delivered people’s care and treatment with them, including what was important and mattered to them. They did this in line with legislation and current evidence-based good practice and standards.

Assessments and care plans were provided in line with current good practice and reflected the principles of Right Care, Right Support and Right Culture. Care was tailored to help people live as independently as possible while receiving the support they needed to remain safe and well. Staff received training relevant to the needs of people using the service and were supported to develop the skills and knowledge required to provide effective care.

People were supported to maintain their nutrition and hydration. Where people required encouragement, prompting or monitoring with eating and drinking, staff provided support in line with their assessed needs. For example, a person told us staff encouraged them to eat and drink when they were reluctant to do so and provided meals and drinks when needed.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: How staff, teams and services work together

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider worked well across teams and services to support people. They made sure people only needed to tell their story once by sharing their assessment of needs when people moved between different services.

The provider participated in multidisciplinary team (MDT) meetings with health and social care professionals to discuss people with complex needs, share relevant information and agree care and treatment plans. Staff also worked in partnership with schools and other services where required. For example, communication care plans were shared to help ensure staff understood people's communication needs and could provide consistent support.

Handovers between staff and teams helped ensure important information about people's needs, risks and preferences was communicated effectively. This collaborative approach supported joined-up care and helped ensure people received consistent support across different services and settings.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Monitoring and improving outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider routinely monitored people’s care and treatment to continuously improve it. They ensured that outcomes were positive and consistent, and that they met both clinical expectations and the expectations of people themselves.

Care records showed people's physical health, wellbeing and mental health were regularly reviewed. The provider participated in multidisciplinary team (MDT) meetings where appropriate and worked with external professionals to review people's progress and agree ongoing support.

People told us staff played an important role in supporting their emotional wellbeing as well as their physical health. A person said, “I wouldn’t be here today if I did not have their practical and emotional support.”

The provider regularly reviewed people's care to assess whether outcomes were being achieved and whether support remained appropriate. Relatives told us staff understood what was important to people and worked towards achieving their goals. A relative explained their aim was for their loved one to remain living at home for as long as possible and told us this had been achieved with the support of staff, who had helped them maintain their independence and quality of life.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Supporting people to live healthier lives

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider supported people to manage their health and wellbeing to maximise their independence, choice and control. Staff supported people to live healthier lives and where possible, reduce their future needs for care and support.

People were supported to access healthcare services and attend appointments, including with GPs, Mental Health Teams (MHT), occupational therapists and other professionals when required. A person told us, “I have the MHT, GP and Social Services involved in my care.” Another person said, “If I was ever unwell the girls would ring for an ambulance and the office and stay with me until it arrives. The carers have also attended GP appointments when I have asked for it.”

Care records demonstrated staff worked with healthcare professionals to support people's health needs. For example, a person at risk of pressure damage was supported with input from district nurses, and staff followed guidance to help maintain their skin integrity and reduce the risk of deterioration.

Staff encouraged people to remain as independent as possible and provided support that reflected their individual needs and preferences, helping people maintain choice and control over their daily lives.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Responsive
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Responsive – this means we looked for evidence that the provider met people’s needs.

At our last assessment we rated this key question requires improvement. At this assessment the rating has changed to good.

This meant people’s needs were met through good organisation and delivery.

topicareas.name: Care provision, Integration and continuity

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider understood the diverse health and care needs of people and their local communities, so care was joined-up, flexible and supported choice and continuity.

People and their relatives valued the continuity of care provided by regular staff who knew them well.

Staff worked with people, relatives and external professionals to provide support that met people’s care and support needs. A relative told us their loved one required “Lots of prompting and patience,” adding that carers understood the importance of working at their pace and providing reliable support. People were also supported to access their local community and participate in activities that were important to them.

People and relatives spoke positively about the care provided and told us staff knew them well. They consistently highlighted the benefits of receiving support from a small, regular team of carers. . A relative said staff understood their loved one’s needs, boundaries and routines, and described staff as patient and reliable.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in access

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider made sure that people could access the care, support and treatment they needed when they needed it.

People and their relatives told us they knew who to contact if they needed additional support or wanted changes made to their care arrangements. They described the service as flexible and responsive to their needs. A person told us, “I have made some changes to my care as well as increasing the visits in the day. I have also changed the times of my morning call. I discussed it with the carer who contacted the office and we agreed the call would be an hour later, which has worked out a lot better for both of us.”

People and relatives were confident that requests for support would be acted upon and that staff and managers were accessible when needed.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in experiences and outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff and leaders actively listened to information about people who are most likely to experience inequality in experience or outcomes and tailored their care, support and treatment in response to this.

People received a service user guide which provided information about the service, the support available and their rights. Assessments and care planning considered people's individual circumstances, needs and desired outcomes to ensure support was personalised and accessible.

Regular care reviews were used to ensure the care people received continued to meet their needs and achieve the outcomes that were important to them. People and, where appropriate, their relatives were involved in these discussions and given opportunities to provide feedback on the support they received.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Listening to and involving people

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider made it easy for people to share feedback and ideas, or raise complaints about their care, treatment and support. Staff involved people in decisions about their care and told them what had changed as a result.

People and relatives told us they felt comfortable raising concerns with staff and management. A person said, “I have not had any reasons to raise any concerns. If I did, I would contact the office. The office staff are very good and always pass on any messages.” A relative told us, “I have never had a need to raise any complaints. If that occasion ever arose, I would speak to the registered manager as they are very easy to talk to, supportive and care.”

The provider sought feedback through regular reviews and spot-check visits, which gave people and their relatives opportunities to share their views about the quality of the service, discuss any concerns and contribute to decisions about their care and support.

Records showed concerns and complaints were reported, logged, investigated and responded to appropriately. The provider maintained oversight of complaints to ensure actions were taken and outcomes were communicated where required. Lessons learned from complaints and concerns were shared with staff to promote learning and support continuous improvement in the quality of care provided.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Person-centred Care

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider made sure people were at the centre of their care and treatment choices and they did not always work in partnership with people, to decide how to respond to any relevant changes in people’s needs.

Care plans contained information about people’s assessed needs and provided staff with guidance on how to support their mental health, physical health and personal care needs. However, we found care records did not always include information about people’s life histories, backgrounds, education, previous occupations, significant relationships and personal experiences. This meant new staff may not always have sufficient information to fully understand the person beyond their care needs.

People and relatives consistently told us staff knew them well and provided personalised support. They described having a regular and consistent team of carers, which helped build trusting relationships and ensured staff understood their individual needs, preferences and routines. Staff we spoke with demonstrated a good understanding of people’s interests, choices and day-to-day routines. Care records also showed staff adapted their support in response to people’s changing wellbeing and preferences.

One person told us, “I have severe mental health problems and require round-the-clock care. I have a team of four carers who rotate, and I get on with them all. We have a very close relationship, and they understand my needs and support me.” This reflected the positive and personalised relationships people had developed with staff who knew them well.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Planning for the future

evidenceCategory.commentary:
People were supported to plan for important life changes, so they could have enough time to make informed decisions about their future, including at the end of their life.

At the time of our assessment, the service was not supporting anyone who was receiving end-of-life care. However, the provider discussed people's future wishes and preferences as part of the assessment and care planning process, helping to ensure people had opportunities to express their views about their future care.

The provider recognised that people's needs may change over time and worked with people, relatives and professionals to plan for these changes. Where people developed specific health needs, the provider told us staff would receive additional training tailored to the person's needs to ensure they could continue to provide safe and appropriate support.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Providing Information

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider supplied appropriate, accurate and up-to-date information in formats that were tailored to individual needs.

The provider told us information could be provided in different formats to meet people's individual communication needs, and systems were available to support accessible communication where required.

People's communication needs were discussed and assessed before care commenced and formed part of the assessment process. Care plans included guidance for staff about how best to communicate with people and ensure they were involved in decisions about their care.

For example, staff supported 1 person who communicated non-verbally. Records described how the person used gestures, body movements and other non-verbal cues to express themselves. Staff demonstrated a good understanding of these communication methods and knew how to recognise and respond to the person's wishes, preferences and wellbeing.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Safe
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Safe – this means we looked for evidence that people were protected from abuse and avoidable harm. At our last assessment we rated this key question requires improvement. At this assessment the rating has changed to good.

This meant people were safe and protected from avoidable harm.

topicareas.name: Infection prevention and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider assessed and managed the risk of infection. They detected and controlled the risk of it spreading and shared concerns with appropriate agencies promptly.

People spoke positively about how staff maintained cleanliness within their homes. A person told us staff put items away and emptied bins after providing support, while another said staff were respectful of their home environment. This demonstrated staff helped maintain clean and tidy living spaces.

Staff received training in infection prevention and control and told us they had access to appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) to carry out their roles safely. Daily care records showed staff used PPE when providing care and support. In addition, staff practice was monitored through spot checks, which included observations of infection prevention and control procedures to ensure staff followed good practice and minimised the risk of infection transmission.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Involving people to manage risks

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider worked well with people to understand and manage risks. Staff provided care to meet people’s needs that was safe, supportive and enabled people to do the things that mattered to them.

Risk assessments were in place and identified risks relating to people’s health, safety and wellbeing. These provided staff with clear guidance on managing risks associated with mobility and transfers, mental health conditions, catheter care and pressure damage. Mental health care plans included information on recognising signs of deterioration or relapse and the actions staff should take in response. However, we noted that potential triggers were not always documented. We discussed this with the registered manager, who assured us this information would be added to strengthen the guidance available to staff.

Staff demonstrated a good understanding of people’s individual needs, including their mental health needs. They were able to describe the early signs of relapse, the support they would provide and when additional professional support would be sought. One staff member explained that a person refusing to eat was often an early indicator of deterioration and described using reassurance, involving relatives, and seeking guidance from the registered manager and mental health team where appropriate. Relatives told us people were supported by a consistent team of carers who knew them well, enabling staff to recognise and respond promptly to changes in people’s wellbeing.

People and relatives consistently told us staff understood individual risks and took appropriate action to keep people safe. One person said staff helped ensure they were “steady on my feet” when supporting them with personal care and bathing. A relative described staff as “very vigilant” and said they were able to recognise when their loved one might be in pain or experiencing difficulties, ensuring support was provided in a timely way.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider had a proactive and positive culture of safety, based on openness and honesty. Staff listened to concerns about safety and investigated and reported safety events. Lessons were learnt to continually identify and embed good practice.

Staff were aware of the systems for reporting incidents and understood the importance of escalating concerns. A staff member told us, “Any incident at all, no matter if it looks small. We always talk to the registered manager about it and maintain a detailed report.”

Records showed incidents were reviewed by the management team and learning was identified where appropriate. For example, when staff identified a potential hazard during a visit, they managed the situation safely, followed the provider’s procedures and informed the person's relative. Learning from the incident highlighted the importance of completing environmental safety checks on arrival and remaining calm when managing potentially risky situations. Staff meetings were used to discuss incidents, identify lessons learned and reinforce good practice.

The provider monitored incidents, reviewed trends and patterns, and used this information to inform risk management and improve practice. Incident records demonstrated that concerns were reviewed, actions were taken and opportunities for learning were considered to help keep people safe.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Medicines optimisation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider made sure that medicines and treatments were safe and met people’s needs, capacities and preferences. Staff involved people in planning, including when changes happened.

People and relatives told us about the support they received with medicines. A person told us staff prompted them to take their medicines as prescribed. Another person explained they managed their own medicines but knew staff could provide support if needed. A relative told us staff ensured their loved one received their medicines as prescribed and said the provider carried out regular medication checks. Another relative explained they chose to manage medicines themselves, although staff were available to assist if required.

Staff received medicines management training, and their competency was assessed to ensure they could administer and support medicines safely. The provider had policies and procedures in place to support safe medicines practice. Records of medicines administration and support provided were maintained. Medicines audits were completed regularly to identify any errors and monitor compliance.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe and effective staffing

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider made sure there were enough qualified, skilled and experienced staff, who received effective support, supervision and development. They worked together well to provide safe care that met people’s individual needs.

People and relatives told us staffing arrangements worked effectively and described care staff as reliable, knowledgeable, punctual and responsive to changing needs.

Staff rotas demonstrated visits were scheduled effectively, with sufficient travel time between calls and no overlap in planned visits. Records showed staff generally spent the allocated duration of visits with people and that people were supported by a consistent group of staff who knew them well.

The provider carried out recruitment checks to ensure staff were suitable to work with people using the service. Staff files contained evidence of employment history checks, explanations for gaps in employment, Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS) checks, references and confirmation of staff's right to work in the UK before employment commenced. However, we found 2 instances where applicants had no previous care experience, references were sometimes obtained from friends or family members. Whilst this provided some assurance about the individual's character, it may not always offer an independent assessment of their suitability for the role. We discussed this with the registered manager, who acknowledged the importance of obtaining references from individuals able to provide objective information about a person's character, conduct and reliability.

Staff told us they felt supported in their roles and had access to training, supervision and development opportunities. A staff member said, “I get monthly supervision. I had 6 weeks training and shadowing for 10 days working alongside an experienced staff member. It was paid.” Training records showed staff had completed a wide range of mandatory and role-specific training, and competency assessments were undertaken to help ensure staff had the knowledge and skills to provide safe care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe environments

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider detected and controlled potential risks in the care environment. They made sure equipment, facilities and technology supported the delivery of safe care.

Environmental risk assessments were completed to identify potential hazards within people's homes and to ensure staff had information about how to work safely. These assessments considered factors within the home environment that could affect the delivery of care and helped staff understand any measures required to reduce risks.

The provider-maintained records of equipment used to support people with their care and mobility needs. Equipment logs showed items such as profiling beds, rollator frames, Sara Stedy transfer aids and other moving and handling equipment had been checked and were within their service or inspection dates. This helped ensure equipment remained safe to use and supported the delivery of safe care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe systems, pathways and transitions

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider worked with people and healthcare partners to establish and maintain safe systems of care, in which safety was managed or monitored. They made sure there was continuity of care, including when people moved between different services.

Prior to accepting a package of care, the registered manager completed an assessment to determine whether the service could safely meet the person's needs. The provider sought additional information when referral information was unclear or incomplete and worked with commissioning teams and social workers to ensure care packages accurately reflected people's needs. Where the provider identified proposed care hours as insufficient to safely support a person, they challenged this and requested reviews or additional provision. The provider also recognised when needs exceeded the scope of the service and did not accept referrals where risks could not be safely managed. For example, the registered manager described declining a referral where a person was at significant risk due to regular self-harming behaviours.

The provider worked collaboratively with external professionals, including social workers and mental health services, to support people's wellbeing and safety.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safeguarding

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider worked with people and healthcare partners to understand what being safe meant to them and the best way to achieve that. Staff concentrated on improving people’s lives while protecting their right to live in safety, free from bullying, harassment, abuse, discrimination, avoidable harm and neglect. The provider shared concerns quickly and appropriately.

People and relatives consistently told us they felt safe with staff and trusted them. A person said, “I feel safe around them as I know them and trust them.” Another person told us, “I trust them and they help me feel safe emotionally.” A relative told us having familiar carers was “pertinent” because their loved one recognised the carers and appeared relaxed and comfortable in their presence.

Staff received safeguarding training and demonstrated an understanding of their responsibilities to protect people from abuse and neglect. They knew how to recognise potential signs of abuse and understood the procedures for raising concerns. The registered manager was knowledgeable about safeguarding processes and worked with relevant health and social care professionals to ensure concerns were acted upon appropriately and people remained safe.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Well-led – this means we looked for evidence that service leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation; and promoted an open, fair culture.

At our last assessment we rated this key question requires improvement. At this assessment the rating has changed to good.

This meant the service was consistently managed and well-led. Leaders and the culture they created promoted high-quality, person-centred care.

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider had inclusive leaders at all levels who understood the context in which they delivered care, treatment and support and embodied the culture and values of their workforce and organisation. Leaders had the skills, knowledge, experience and credibility to lead effectively. They did so with integrity, openness and honesty.

People and relatives spoke positively about the management of the service. A person told us, “I find the manager easy to talk to, communication is good. If I text or email, they always respond.” Another person said, “I find the manager extremely supportive, a great listener and always willing to help.”

Staff consistently described the registered manager as approachable, knowledgeable and supportive. A staff member told us, “The registered manager is knowledgeable and always supportive. She is easy to talk to.” Another said, “The registered manager is very thorough, respectful and approachable. She is fully invested in the good. She monitors and checks on us and gives her time to make things right.”

Feedback from people, relatives and staff demonstrated the registered manager was visible, understood their role and promoted a positive culture focused on achieving good outcomes for people.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider fostered a positive culture where people felt they could speak up and their voice would be heard.

Staff consistently described the registered manager as approachable and supportive. A staff member told us, “The registered manager always listens and I feel I can share my views.” Another said, “The registered manager listens and she is genuinely caring and interested in people. I can speak to her about anything.”

Regular team meetings provided staff with opportunities to discuss concerns, share feedback and raise any issues affecting their work. This helped create an open culture where staff felt comfortable expressing their views and contributing to service improvement.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider had clear responsibilities, roles, systems of accountability or good governance. They acted on the best information about risk, performance and outcomes, or share this securely with others when appropriate.

The provider completed a range of audits and risk assessments covering key areas of the service. Systems were in place to monitor incidents, complaints, compliments and other quality indicators, enabling the provider to identify trends and patterns and take action where required. The provider also commissioned an external compliance company to independently review and monitor the service. Regular audits and assessments were undertaken across all aspects of the service to evaluate effectiveness, identify areas for improvement and provide additional oversight.

Care call monitoring audits were used to review attendance, punctuality and the quality of care delivery. Records showed attendance levels were high, with most people receiving all scheduled visits. A missed visit was identified during the audit period, which had been reviewed and learning identified.

The provider carried out regular audits of care records to monitor the quality and accuracy of documentation and to ensure staff reported incidents, concerns and changes in people’s needs appropriately. Where areas for improvement were identified, actions were taken through supervision, training and staff support.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider focused on continuous learning, innovation and improvement across the organisation and local system. They encouraged creative ways of delivering equality of experience, outcome and quality of life for people. They actively contributed to safe, effective practice and research.

The provider worked with an external compliance company to review the quality of the service and identify areas for improvement. Action plans were developed and monitored to support continuous improvement and maintain high standards of care.

The registered manager told us they were part of local provider networks and forums, where registered managers shared best practice, discussed challenges and supported one another. They also attended relevant webinars, training events and sector updates to keep their knowledge current and ensure the service responded to changes in legislation, guidance and best practice.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider understood their duty to collaborate and work in partnership, so services worked seamlessly for people. They shared information and learning with partners and collaborated for improvement.

The provider worked closely with GPs, community nurses, mental health services, social workers, occupational therapists and other professionals involved in people's care. Information was shared appropriately to ensure care remained responsive to people's changing needs and to support continuity of care.

The provider also worked with external training providers and sector partners to develop staff knowledge and skills. This helped ensure staff were equipped to provide safe, effective and person-centred care. Through partnership working and information sharing, the provider contributed to improving people's experiences and achieving positive outcomes.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider had a shared vision, strategy and culture. This was based on transparency, equity, equality and human rights, diversity and inclusion, engagement, and understanding challenges and the needs of people and their communities.

People and their relatives spoke highly of the service and the support they received. A person told us, “I would struggle without the support from Best2Care, and I wouldn’t know what would happen to me or what place I would be in without their help. I find them very supportive and overall, very happy with the service I receive.” Another person said, “The company provide me with stability and having the same team of carers is very good for me. I don’t feel there is anything they could improve on.”

Relatives also described a positive and caring culture. A relative told us, “Best2Care are a fantastic company and I feel very privileged and can’t thank the staff enough for what they do for my loved one and the support they give to me as well. The set up works really well.”

Staff feedback reflected the provider's values and commitment to delivering high-quality care. A staff member told us, “Working with Best2Care has broadened my knowledge and understanding in care and the needs of people with mental health conditions.” Staff consistently spoke positively about the support they received and their ability to provide person-centred care.

The provider promoted its vision and values through induction, training, staff meetings, team meetings and social events. Staff were provided with a staff handbook when they started employment, and regular communication and team meetings to reinforced the standards and, behaviours.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider valued diversity in their workforce. They worked towards an inclusive and fair culture by improving equality and equity for people who worked for them.

The provider promoted staff wellbeing and fostered inclusion through regular team meetings, social events and ongoing support from managers. Staff were supported to gain recognised qualifications, including Levels 2, 3 and 4 in Health and Social Care, as well as further study opportunities.

Staff told us the registered manager treated them with respect and valued their contributions equally.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care
