asgRatings.title: Ongoing Assessment for Beersheba Social Care Services Limited
asgRatings.name: Homecare
asgRatings.commentary:
We carried out this assessment between 8 and 19 May 2026. Beersheba Social Care Services Limited is a care at home agency that provides personal care to people living in their own homes. CQC only inspects where people are receiving the regulated activity personal care. This is help with tasks related to personal hygiene and eating. Where they do, we consider any wider social care provided.

At the time of this inspection 3 people were receiving support with personal care. This was the first inspection since this service registered with CQC. This service had a registered manager in place.

The service provided care that was safe, effective and centred around people’s individual needs. There were systems in place to monitor care delivery and promote people’s safety. Risks were assessed and addressed in care plans. Care was planned in line with people’s needs and was reviewed when required to ensure it remained appropriate. Staff were trained to be effective in their roles. Staff understood their roles and responsibilities and knew how to escalate concerns. They were supported through regular support and supervisions. The registered manager monitored staff performance through spot checks and observation. They maintained regular contact and communication with staff which helped to promote consistency in how care was delivered.

The registered manager involved other healthcare services where required to ensure people’s needs were met. They worked in partnership with other services to develop and improve the service.

The provider demonstrated a commitment to delivering good quality care. they had systems and processes to monitor the service.
asgRatings.narrative: The service is performing well and meeting our expectations.
asgRatings.overallPeopleExperience:
People and their relatives were generally positive about the service. They described care as reliable, respectful and responsive. They told us staff supported them to maintain their independence and made sure care was centred around their choices and preferences. People said staff took time to understand how they wanted things done and adapted their approach to meet their needs.

People described staff as kind, patient and reassuring. They told us staff were attentive and responsive, noticing when they were uncomfortable or anxious and acting quickly to provide support. One person said staff were “Very careful and do things thoroughly” and had quickly learnt how to support them in the way they preferred. People felt staff listened to them and understood how they communicated, which helped to build trusting relationships.

Continuity of care was valued by people, with regular staff who knew them well. People said this meant staff understood their routines, preferences and needs. One person told us, “We have established a routine of how I like things done and it’s working.”

People felt respected in their own homes and said staff maintained their privacy and dignity, particularly when they had visitors. They told us staff went “The extra mile” and were always “Positive and reassuring,” with nothing being too much trouble.

People and relatives felt able to raise concerns or provide feedback and said these were responded to promptly. One person told us they knew who to contact and felt issues were resolved quickly. Care planning was carried out with people, ensuring their views were reflected in how care was delivered.

keyQuestionRatings.name: Caring
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Caring – this means we looked for evidence that the provider involved people and treated them with compassion, kindness, dignity and respect.

This is the first assessment for this newly registered service. This key question has been rated good.

This meant people were supported and treated with dignity and respect; and involved as partners in their care.

topicareas.name: Independence, choice and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider promoted people’s independence, so people knew their rights and had choice and control over their own care, treatment and wellbeing.

People told us staff encouraged them to maintain their independence and adapted their support to meet their individual needs. One person said, “Staff come up with other ways of helping me so I can have some independence and reduce discomfort.” They added, “They give me choice. Never have they done anything for me without asking what I want. It’s always about me and my choice.”

Another person told us, “Staff help me with my personal care. They help me go out a lot. I’m grateful for that. Most agencies couldn’t do that. They help me do the things I want to do. Staff only come on the days and times I need them. I decide and let them know.”

Care plans were person-centred and reflected people’s needs, choices and preferences. People confirmed they were involved in planning their care and that their wishes were respected in how support was delivered.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Kindness, compassion and dignity

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider always treated people with kindness, empathy and compassion and respected their privacy and dignity. Staff treated colleagues from other organisations with kindness and respect.

People spoke positively about how staff supported them in a considerate and respectful way within their own homes. One person told us, “My friends visit me and they give me space and privacy. They find other things to do in the house. They go the extra mile. I'm so thankful to them. They are wonderful.” They also added, “They are lovely with lovely personalities. Always patient, kind and considerate of my needs and my family and always respectful to us and our home.” Another person told us, “They are respectful and understanding.” These comments demonstrated staff consistently treated people with dignity and respect, while being mindful of their privacy and personal environment.

Staff were supported through training and observations to ensure they maintained and promoted people’s dignity.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Responding to people’s immediate needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider listened to and understood people’s needs, views and wishes. Staff responded to people’s needs in the moment and acted to minimise any discomfort, concern or distress.

People told us staff were attentive, observant and responsive. One person said, “The amount of attention and detail they give is so good. They are very careful and do things thoroughly.” They explained that although there had initially been some difficulty with how staff supported them, staff quickly understood their preferences. They added, “They are observant and can tell when I'm uncomfortable or stressed and they respond quickly.”

Staff demonstrated flexibility in responding to people’s changing needs. Care needs assessments considered people’s physical and emotional needs, as well as factors that could affect their emotional wellbeing. This supported staff to provide care that was responsive and personalised.

People and their relatives also spoke positively about the support provided by the management team. One person said, “They are always very positive and reassuring and that's what I need. Nothing is too much for them to help me with.”

One relative told us, “Anytime we call for help, the registered manager and operations manager come as soon as they can. They provide so much support to us and always listen to us.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Treating people as individuals

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider treated people as individuals and made sure people’s care, support and treatment met people’s needs and preferences. They took account of people’s strengths, abilities, aspirations, culture and unique backgrounds and protected characteristics.

People’s care plans contained relevant information about their personal circumstances, including religion, cultural needs and other individual preferences. Records showed how people preferred to be addressed, and staff understood and respected these choices. For example, a person’s care plan outlined how they wished to be supported to follow their religious practices. Another care plan detailed how the person preferred to receive support with specific personal care tasks.

People confirmed care was delivered in line with their preferences. One person told us, “We have established a routine of how I like things done and it’s working.” Another person said, “My friends visit me often and they give me space and privacy to be with them. They find other things to do in the house. They are always very positive and reassuring and that’s what I need. Nothing is too much for them to help me with.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce wellbeing and enablement

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider cared about and promoted the wellbeing of their staff and supported and enabled staff to always deliver person-centred care.

Staff had access to additional support through a dedicated helpline, which they could use if they experienced any personal or work-related concerns. The management team maintained regular contact with staff to check on their wellbeing, including how they were coping and feeling in their roles. Flexible rotas were also in place to support staff in achieving a positive work-life balance.

The registered manager provided additional support to staff where needed. For example, staff new to the country and working under a Certificate of Sponsorship were regularly checked on to ensure they were settling into their roles and coping with their work and environment. This demonstrated a supportive and inclusive approach to staff wellbeing.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Effective
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Effective – this means we looked for evidence that people’s care, treatment and support achieved good outcomes and promoted a good quality of life, based on best available evidence.

This is the first assessment for this newly registered service. This key question has been rated good.

This meant people’s outcomes were consistently good, and people’s feedback confirmed this.

topicareas.name: Assessing needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider made sure people’s care and treatment was effective by assessing and reviewing their health, care, wellbeing and communication needs with them.

The registered manager assessed people’s needs prior to them starting to use the service.

People spoke positively about their involvement in the assessment process. One person told us, “[Registered manager] met with me to discuss my needs and what I wanted. They listened to me.” Another person said, “The registered manager spent hours with us discussing all aspects of my needs and my health. We have had a meeting recently to discuss possible changes and how they can support us.”

Assessments covered a range of areas including people’s medical conditions, physical and mental health, mobility, nutrition and social needs. Input from relevant professionals was sought where required to ensure people received appropriate and coordinated care. Care plans were developed based on these assessments and reflected peoples identified needs, supporting the delivery of effective and personalised care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Consent to care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider told people about their rights around consent and respected these when delivering person-centred care and treatment.

People told us staff always sought their consent in all areas of care and respected their choices.

People were actively involved in the care planning process and supported to make decisions about their care. Where people required additional support, staff worked with advocates and ensured relevant information was provided so decisions were made in people’s best interests.

One staff member told us, “I understand everyone has the right to make choices. Even if they can’t express this themselves, they still have that right. I make sure they get the information they need, involve an advocate if required, and explain the risks and benefits so they can make informed decisions.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Delivering evidence-based care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider planned and delivered people’s care and treatment with them, including what was important and mattered to them. They did this in line with legislation and current evidence-based good practice and standards.

People’s nutritional and hydration needs were assessed and clearly documented. Care plans provided detailed guidance for staff on the support people required with preparing food, including any specific dietary needs such as modified food textures, nutritional supplements and feeding plans. Staff demonstrated they followed this guidance in practice, supporting people consistently and safely.

This approach ensured people received coordinated and effective care that reflected best practice, helping to maintain their health and wellbeing and mitigate potential risks.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: How staff, teams and services work together

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider worked well across teams and services to support people. They made sure people only needed to tell their story once by sharing their assessment of needs when people moved between different services. The provider worked effectively with other teams and services to support people’s health and wellbeing.

People told us they were supported to access the services and equipment they needed. One person described how the registered manager had supported them to obtain appropriate equipment and access relevant healthcare services to meet their needs. Another person told us the service continued to liaise with a range of professionals to ensure their healthcare needs were met.

Information was shared appropriately with other services and agencies involved in people’s care. Staff worked collaboratively with other professionals and attended meetings where they contributed feedback and followed agreed actions. This meant people did not have to repeatedly share their history when moving between services, supporting continuity of care and a more seamless experience.

The registered manager supported people to make referrals to external services where required. People confirmed staff supported them to attend healthcare appointments when needed, helping to ensure they received timely and appropriate care and treatment.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Monitoring and improving outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider routinely monitored people’s care and treatment to continuously improve it. They ensured that outcomes were positive and consistent, and that they met both clinical expectations and the expectations of people themselves.

The provider regularly contacted people to gather feedback and check on the quality of care delivered. This enabled the provider to identify any issues promptly and take appropriate action to improve outcomes for people.

The registered manager also visited people to carry out observations of staff practice. These checks ensured staff were following people’s care plans and meeting their needs as intended. Care plans clearly described the outcomes people wished to achieve from their care. One person told us, “They are helping me a lot to do the things I want like going out and visits to leisure centres.” This demonstrated how care was planned and delivered in a way that supported people to achieve their goals and maintain their independence.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Supporting people to live healthier lives

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider supported people to manage their health and wellbeing to maximise their independence, choice and control. Staff supported people to live healthier lives and where possible, reduce their future needs for care and support.

Records showed, and people confirmed, that staff supported them to maintain their health and wellbeing by accessing healthcare services and following advice from professionals. One person told us, “The carers often accompany me to my GP and hospital appointments if I ask.”

Staff followed professional guidance to ensure people’s needs were met. For example, staff supported people to carry out prescribed physical exercises, followed individual nutrition plans and adhered to instructions for the safe administration of medicines. This helped to ensure people received consistent care that promoted their ongoing health and independence.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Responsive
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Responsive – this means we looked for evidence that the provider met people’s needs.

This is the first assessment for this newly registered service. This key question has been rated good.

This meant people’s needs were met through good organisation and delivery.

topicareas.name: Care provision, Integration and continuity

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider understood the diverse health and care needs of people and their local communities, so care was joined-up, flexible and supported choice and continuity.

Staff worked creatively to support people to achieve their personal goals and maintain independence. For example, one person was supported to attend a local leisure centre to help improve and maintain their mobility. The service also worked in partnership with another agency to support a person to maintain and continue their employment.

Staff supported people to take part in activities they enjoyed for relaxation and stimulation. This included ensuring people could watch television programmes they liked and supporting people to meet their religious and spiritual needs by enabling them to take part in relevant activities or practices.

The provider-maintained continuity within the care team wherever possible, which helped people to build trusting and meaningful relationships with staff. Support provided took account of people’s physical, emotional, social and family needs, and extending support to individuals and their families to promote wellbeing and continuity of care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in access

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider made sure that people could access the care, support and treatment they needed when they needed it.

Care delivery was flexible, with visit times adjusted to meet people’s preferences and changing needs. Staff supported people in a responsive and flexible way and attended to requests for urgent or emergency support to help ensure people’s safety and wellbeing. People and their relatives confirmed they were able to reach out to the service and contact staff when they needed additional support.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in experiences and outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff and leaders actively listened to information about people who are most likely to experience inequality in experience or outcomes and tailored their care, support and treatment in response to this.

The registered manager demonstrated a good understanding of people’s diverse needs and ensured care was delivered in a person‑centred way, helping to improve people’s experiences and outcomes. An open and transparent system of communication was promoted, which helped ensure people felt listened to and supported, and that feedback was used to inform improvements to the service.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Listening to and involving people

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider made it easy for people to share feedback and ideas, or raise complaints about their care, treatment and support. Staff involved people in decisions about their care and told them what had changed as a result.

The provider actively sought feedback from people and their relatives through surveys and regular review meetings. They also operated systems that enabled people to share their views about the service at any time. Open communication was promoted, which helped people and their families feel confident raising concerns. We saw that concerns were responded to promptly and resolved wherever possible.

The service had a complaints procedure in place, and people and their relatives were provided with a copy when they first started using the service. People told us they understood how to raise concerns and felt comfortable doing so. One person said they would speak directly to the registered manager if they had any concerns and trusted them to take action. They commented, “[The registered manager] is very good. If I have any problems, she will sort it out quickly.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Person-centred Care

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider made sure people were at the centre of their care and treatment choices and they decided, in partnership with people, how to respond to any relevant changes in people’s needs.

People’s individual needs were met through detailed care plans, which covered a range of areas including personal care, nutrition, skin care, mobility and transfers, social activities and physical health needs. Care plans also included information about people’s background, communication needs, likes and dislikes, hobbies and interests. Clear guidance was provided on how to support people with specific tasks and activities in line with their individual preferences and requirements.

People spoke positively about the personalised care they received. One person told us, “The carers are careful and always put me and how I like things done in mind. They listen and follow my preferences. They know how to support me.”

Staff completed daily care records which detailed the support people received. A relative confirmed this and told us, “My relative is very well cared for. [The registered manager] and the staff are thorough. They understand my relative’s needs.” Care plans were reviewed regularly and updated as required to reflect changes in people’s needs, helping to ensure care remained safe, responsive and person centred.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Planning for the future

evidenceCategory.commentary:
People were supported to plan for important life changes, so they could have enough time to make informed decisions about their future, including at the end of their life.

At the time of our inspection, the service was not supporting anyone with end‑of‑life care. The registered manager told us that discussions about people’s wishes and preferences in this area were included as part of care reviews, where appropriate, and involved people and their relatives. This approach ensured people were supported to make informed choices if and when they wished to discuss future care planning.

The registered manager explained that people’s wishes would be respected and documented in care plans, and appropriate support put in place to meet their needs. They demonstrated an understanding of when and how to involve other health and social care professionals to ensure people received coordinated and appropriate support should end‑of‑life care be required.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Providing Information

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider supplied appropriate, accurate and up-to-date information in formats that were tailored to individual needs.

Care plans included detailed information about people’s communication needs and how staff should support them effectively. These also recorded people’s preferred methods of communication, such as whether they wished to be contacted by email or telephone.

Staff adjusted their communication approaches to meet people’s needs, including how information was explained to support understanding. They used basic words and gestures to promote effective communication where necessary. Care records identified any barriers to effective communication and outlined actions staff should take to minimise these. This helped ensure people were involved in their care and able to make informed decisions.

At the time of our inspection, there was no one using the service who required information in alternative languages or formats. However, the provider told us they were able and willing to work with other agencies, including translation services, to support people should such needs arise.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Safe
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Safe – this means we looked for evidence that people were protected from abuse and avoidable harm.

This is the first assessment for this newly registered service. This key question has been rated good.

This meant people were safe and protected from avoidable harm.

topicareas.name: Infection prevention and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider assessed and managed the risk of infection. They detected and controlled the risk of it spreading and shared concerns with appropriate agencies promptly.

People were protected from the risk of infection. The service had clear infection prevention and control policies and procedures in place, and staff had completed training to ensure they understood their responsibilities. People and relatives confirmed that staff followed infection control practices and used personal protective equipment appropriately.

Staff used personal protective equipment (PPE), such as gloves and aprons, safely and correctly when providing care and support. The registered manager carried out practice observations to monitor staff compliance with infection prevention and control procedures and to ensure these were followed consistently. This oversight helped maintain safe standards of care and reduced the risk of infection for people using the service.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Involving people to manage risks

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider worked with people to understand and manage risks by thinking holistically. Staff provided care to meet people’s needs that was safe, supportive and enabled people to do the things that mattered to them.

Individual risk assessments were completed and covered areas such as people’s physical health conditions, risks of pressure damage, nutrition, moving and handling, and risks associated with specific health needs. Risk assessments and management plans detailed how staff should support people safely and reduce any risks associated with their health conditions and care delivery while continuing to support people’s independence.

People and their relatives confirmed that staff followed guidance and supported them in a way that promoted safety and wellbeing. Staff discussed risks with people and, where appropriate, their relatives, and agreed how risks should be managed.

Appropriate equipment was available to support people safely with moving and transfers when required. An occupational therapist had been involved in assessing people’s moving and positioning needs and in developing moving and positioning plans. They also supported staff training to ensure care was delivered safely and promoted the safety of both people and staff.

Risk management plans were reviewed and updated regularly to reflect changes in people’s needs or circumstances, helping to ensure care remained safe, responsive and person centred.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider had a proactive and positive culture of safety, based on openness and honesty. Staff listened to concerns about safety and investigated and reported safety events. Lessons were learnt to continually identify and embed good practice.

Staff felt confident to raise concerns and understood their responsibility to report incidents, accidents and near misses relating to people’s care. These were reported to the registered manager, who reviewed them promptly and took appropriate action to reduce risks and prevent recurrence. For example, following concerns about a person’s choking risk, the registered manager updated the person’s care plan and risk assessment to ensure guidance reflected the identified risk and required support. The registered manager and staff held regular discussions and updates to review incidents, concerns and near misses. Learning from these was shared with staff to improve the care delivered to people.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Medicines optimisation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider made sure that medicines and treatments were safe and met people’s needs, capacities and preferences. Staff involved people in planning, including when changes happened.

The provider had safe systems and processes in place for the administration and management of medicines. People confirmed staff supported them to take their medicines safely. Staff had received training in the safe administration and management of medicines, and their competency was regularly assessed to ensure safe practice. Medicines administration records were completed accurately. Care plans set out the support people required with their medicines, and staff followed this guidance to ensure medicines were administered as prescribed.

The registered manager carried out regular audits of medicines records to identify any issues or discrepancies. This oversight helped ensure medicines were managed safely and any concerns were addressed promptly, reducing the risk of errors and promoting positive outcomes for people using the service.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe and effective staffing

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider made sure there were enough qualified, skilled and experienced staff, who received effective support, supervision and development. They worked together well to provide safe care that met people’s individual needs.

People and their relatives confirmed staffing arrangements were reliable and responsive. One person told us, “They are here when they should be and they support me well. If they are running late, they always let us know. We have never had a time that they did not show up.” A relative said, “The carers are good. They are competent in their roles and I believe they have had the right training.” The service had a team of staff available to cover visits as required, which helped maintain continuity and reduce missed calls. One person confirmed, “I always do double up for a client as we use hoist and there are always 2 of us.”

Staff received appropriate training and supervision to carry out their roles effectively. All staff completed an induction when they started, which included mandatory training, shadowing experienced staff and competency assessments. Records showed staff had completed training relevant to their roles and responsibilities.

Staff told us they were well supported through regular supervision, observation, spot checks, performance review meetings and opportunities for reflective practice. One member of staff said, “The [registered manager] is available to support me with anything I need. I feel well supported by them.”

The provider followed safe recruitment practices. Staff had completed the required pre‑employment checks before starting work, including references, criminal record checks, verification of employment history, proof of identity and confirmation of the right to work in the UK. These measures helped ensure people were supported by staff who were suitable to work with them.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe environments

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider detected and controlled potential risks in the care environment. They made sure equipment, facilities and technology supported the delivery of safe care.

Individual risk assessments for people’s homes were completed, including fire safety assessments. Equipment, facilities, and technology were checked regularly to ensure they were safe, well maintained, and supported the delivery of safe care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe systems, pathways and transitions

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider worked with people and healthcare partners to establish and maintain safe systems of care, in which safety was managed or monitored. They made sure there was continuity of care, including when people moved between different services.The provider had a system they followed to screen referrals which included assessing people’s needs before people started using the service. As part of this process, staff met with individuals and, where appropriate, their families to discuss needs, preferences and risks, ensuring care could be planned safely and effectively.

The provider worked collaboratively with external professionals to support people’s health and wellbeing. For example, staff worked alongside a dietitian and occupational therapist to ensure the right level of support and equipment was available for people. They worked with other agencies and services involved to get handovers, relevant information and guidance on how to support people appropriately.

People were supported to complete referrals to other services when required, which helped ensure access to appropriate care and reduced the risk of delays or gaps in support. These arrangements promoted joined‑up working, continuity of care and safer outcomes for people using the service.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safeguarding

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider worked with people and healthcare partners to understand what being safe meant to them and the best way to achieve that. Staff concentrated on improving people’s lives while protecting their right to live in safety, free from bullying, harassment, abuse, discrimination, avoidable harm and neglect. The provider shared concerns quickly and appropriately.

People and their relatives told us they felt safe with staff. One person said, “I totally feel safe with all the carers. They are lovely.”

The provider had effective systems and processes in place to safeguard people from abuse, including a safeguarding policy and procedure for staff to follow if they had concerns. Staff had received training to help them identify different types of abuse and neglect. Staff understood the actions they needed to take if they had concerns and knew how to report these appropriately. They were also aware of whistleblowing procedures and understood how to raise concerns with external agencies if required to protect people.

The registered manager demonstrated a clear understanding of their safeguarding responsibilities including notifying and involving other organisations where necessary.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Well-led – this means we looked for evidence that service leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation; and promoted an open, fair culture.

This is the first assessment for this newly registered service. This key question has been rated good.

This meant the service was consistently managed and well-led. Leaders and the culture they created promoted high-quality, person-centred care.

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider had inclusive leaders at all levels who understood the context in which they delivered care, treatment and support and embodied the culture and values of their workforce and organisation. Leaders had the skills, knowledge, experience and credibility to lead effectively. They did so with integrity, openness and honesty.

The registered manager, who was also the nominated individual, had experience of delivering and managing care services. The operations manager was also a director. Both the registered manager and the operations manager were actively involved in the day‑to‑day running of the service, including providing hands‑on care and leadership to staff. They demonstrated a clear understanding of their responsibilities under the duty of candour.

Staff told us they felt supported in their roles and had clear direction and leadership from the registered manager. Staff were appropriately trained to provide effective care to people and understood the importance of sharing information, raising concerns and reporting incidents in line with the provider’s procedures.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider fostered a positive culture where people felt they could speak up and their voice would be heard.

Staff demonstrated a good understanding of their right to raise concerns and were aware of the provider’s freedom to speak up policy. The registered manager actively encouraged an open discussion and regularly provided opportunities for staff to share feedback, raise concerns and discuss any issues affecting their work.

There were a range of accessible avenues in place to enable staff to speak up, which included team meetings, one -to-one and staff having access to the directors of the service and the provider external HR provider.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider had clear responsibilities, roles, systems of accountability and good governance. They used these to manage and deliver good quality, sustainable care, treatment and support. They acted on the best information about risk, performance and outcomes, and shared this securely with others when appropriate.

The provider had a range of policies and procedures in place to support the effective running of the organisation. These were available to staff and provided clear guidance on expected practice.

Governance systems included regular management meetings, where leaders discussed the day-to-day running of the service, business development and the quality of care being delivered. This provided oversight and ensured that issues were identified and addressed in a timely way.

Quality assurance processes were in place to monitor standards and staff practice. These included spot checks, recruitment file audits, assessments of staff competency and regular audits of daily care records. The provider used the results of these checks and audits to identify learning, address shortfalls and support continuous improvement within the service.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider focused on continuous learning, innovation and improvement across the organisation and local system. They encouraged creative ways of delivering equality of experience, outcome and quality of life for people. They actively contributed to safe, effective practice and research.

The provider had a business and development plan in place and used a variety of approaches to support the growth and sustainability of the service. The registered manager told us they attended care roadshows, local authority care forums and worked closely with local service commissioners. They explained that these opportunities enabled them to learn from other providers, share ideas and ensure commissioners were aware of the service and its approach to care delivery.

The registered manager had also subscribed to Skills for Care and Social Care TV. They told us these resources provided access to up‑to‑date guidance, learning materials and training opportunities to support staff development and improve practice.

The provider had taken a proactive approach to workforce planning and had recruited additional staff to ensure capacity was available to respond to increases in demand and support the ongoing delivery of safe, effective care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider understood their duty to collaborate and work in partnership, so services worked seamlessly for people. They shared information and learning with partners and collaborated for improvement.

The service worked in partnership with a range of external agencies, including the Department for Work and Pensions, health and social care professionals, housing providers and community-based services. These partnerships supported people to receive coordinated, person‑centred care that met their individual needs and helped the provider to further develop and improve the service.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider had a shared vision, strategy and culture. This was based on transparency, equity, equality and human rights, diversity and inclusion, engagement, and understanding challenges and the needs of people and their communities.

The provider’s vision was to deliver compassionate care and support people on a one-to-one basis, working in partnership with other agencies to ensure care was tailored to individual needs.

People spoke positively about the quality of care they received and told us the service met their needs. One person said, “They have done an amazing job in the way they have supported me and are still supporting me. It shows they are truly compassionate.” This feedback reflected the provider’s stated values and vision.

The vision and values of the service were shared with staff during induction and were discussed regularly at staff meetings. Staff we spoke with demonstrated a good understanding of the service’s values and how these guided their day-to-day practice. People and, where appropriate, their relatives confirmed that staff worked in a way that promoted compassion, respect and person-centred care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider valued diversity in their workforce. They worked towards an inclusive and fair culture by improving equality and equity for people who worked for them.

Staff had completed equality and diversity training and demonstrated an understanding of inclusive practice. Staff told us they felt supported in their roles, were given opportunities to develop, and felt listened to by leaders. This helped to promote a positive working environment where staff felt valued and respected.

The provider valued diversity in their workforce. They worked towards an inclusive and fair culture by improving equality and equity for people who worked for them.

Staff had completed equality and diversity training and demonstrated an understanding of inclusive practice. Staff told us they felt supported in their roles, were given opportunities to develop, and felt listened to by leaders. This helped to promote a positive working environment where staff felt valued and respected.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care
